query:
You are reviewing a draft plan, attached as README.md, for choosing the seed (initial) experiments of a closed-loop Bayesian optimization over a function network (BOFN / p-KGFN) campaign that looks for new LPBF aluminium alloys. Also attached: seeds.csv (points already planned), seed_design.py (space-filling picks around those points: Sobol, Sobol with an exclusion radius, greedy maximin, greedy integrated-variance reduction), space_filling_compare.csv (its output), budget_split_sim.py (a toy flat-GP simulation of splitting 25 runs between seeds and qLogEI batches of 3), and its summary.csv and paired_vs_333.csv.

Earlier, you reviewed the original "3 baselines + 3 agent-chosen + 3 space-filling seeds out of 25 runs" idea and recommended about 7 seeds with Kennard-Stone maximin augmentation. The draft agrees on about 6-7 seeds but recommends integrated-variance (IMSE) picks instead of maximin, because in its tests maximin put every point on several composition caps at once.

Please act as a critical reviewer and answer briefly and concretely:
1. Is anything in the draft wrong, overstated or internally inconsistent? Quote the sentence and say what to change.
2. Check seed_design.py and budget_split_sim.py for bugs or choices that bias the conclusions. Examples: the distance and feature scaling, the element-set term, the min-total filter, the IMSE implementation and its length scale, how the agent and baseline seeds are generated, the paired comparison, and whether qLogEI over a discrete pool is a fair stand-in. Run them if you can.
3. Is the IMSE-versus-maximin disagreement resolved correctly? Under what conditions would you still prefer maximin?
4. Do the proposed seed set (D1, D2, B30, a changed B15, S1 = Al-4Mn-0.5Ti-0.5Zr, S2 = an Fe-based eutectic or Al-10Ce, S3/S4 space-filling) and its feedstock caveats make sense for the campaign's goal: stronger than AlSi10Mg and/or as strong as Scalmalloy with less critical-mineral content?
5. What is missing that the team will regret before the first optimizer batch on Dec 18?

Keep the answer under about 1,500 words and finish with a prioritized list of changes.
task_summary: Critically Review Draft Seed Selection And Simulations For BOFN Aluminum Alloy Optimization Campaign

============================== README.md ==============================

# Seeding the BOFN campaign: which experiments come first (#275)

[#275](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/275) asks how to choose the
initial experiments for the Al alloy campaign in
[#255](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/255), which
[#256](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/256) schedules. It suggests
a mix of three sources, about three runs each:

- **agent-chosen** compositions (literature, databases, CALPHAD);
- **known baselines** (AlSi10Mg, Scalmalloy);
- **Sobol** or another space-filling design.

It also asks:

- how to bring in the databases from [#7](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/7)
  and [#8](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/8);
- how "fantasy" data (synthetic, or from the literature) could stand in until real data exist;
- whether 3 + 3 + 3 makes sense with 25 experiments left.

Edison Scientific was the rubber duck: two `LITERATURE_HIGH` reviews and a critique of this
draft. They're in [`edison/`](edison/).

**Status:** this is a plan. Nothing here has been run on a real sample. The compositions are
proposals. They still need the CALPHAD screen, the design-space freeze, and a check of what is
actually on the shelf.

## Short answers

**On 3 + 3 + 3 with 25 left:** keep the three-way mix, but use about 6–7 seeds rather than 9. Give
the runs this frees up to the optimizer.

- **Edison's verdict on 9 seeds is "slightly too many".** Nine seeds are 36 % of the 25 runs.
  Bossek et al. (2020, [10.1145/3377930.3390155](https://doi.org/10.1145/3377930.3390155)) found
  that an initial design of about 30 % of the budget did best on their benchmark suite. Edison
  suggests 3 baselines, 2 agent picks, 2 space-filling points, 14 optimizer runs and 4 finalist
  runs ([q1](edison/q1-seeding-strategy/artifact-00.md)).
- **A toy simulation agrees on the direction** ([below](#how-many-seeds-a-toy-check)). Across 60
  paired problem instances, 2 baselines + 3 agent + 1 space-filling beat 3 + 3 + 3 by
  0.043 ± 0.014 in the best value found. It beat the best baseline 75 % of the time, against
  55 % for 3 + 3 + 3. 3 + 3 + 3 did worst of all the optimizer splits when the agent picks only
  pointed back at the known alloy family. That is the circularity risk Edison also flags.
- **Don't add a third baseline run.** The 6063 runs (A1–A5) and commercial AlSi10Mg powder at P1
  are baselines that cost no design run. D1-r stays: it measures the benchmark's own spread
  ([#256](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/blob/claude/issue-256-20261112-2149/al-campaign-schedule/README.md#the-36-al-runs)).

**In the schedule's terms** ([table](#a-proposed-seed-set)):

- D1 and D2 are the baselines.
- S1–S2 are agent picks, with different strengthening mechanisms.
- S3–S4 are space-filling picks from [`seed_design.py`](seed_design.py), made after the CALPHAD
  screen trims the candidate pool.
- B30 stays a dosing check. B15 should check the element the agent picks depend on (Mn, or Zr)
  rather than Si a second time.
- If the flex slots X1–X3 (Dec 14–16) aren't needed to redo failed runs, use them as early
  optimizer picks, not as more seeds.

**What matters more than the split:**

1. **The optimizer picks R1 (Dec 18) and R2 (Jan 8) before any new composition has strength
   data.** Seed tensile bars print at P3 (Jan 12–13). Until then, the strength nodes run on
   priors. So the literature data and strength models that go into those priors decide the first
   six optimizer runs ([pseudo-data](#literature-and-fantasy-data)).
2. **Most of the literature's best Sc-free seeds need Zr, Fe, Ce or Cu.** None of these is on
   the Nov 13 list in [#146](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/146#issuecomment-6842840090)
   (Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Mg, Sc, Er, Ti from ESPI; Si, Fe, Ni and Cu were never ordered). The
   Scalmalloy-type benchmark D2 needs Zr as well. Check whether Zr is coming. If not, order it as
   an Al–Zr master alloy before the S runs (Dec 7–10).
3. **The design box on [PR #72](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/pull/72)
   excludes several of the best-documented Sc-free LPBF alloys:** Al–10Ce (Ce cap 6 wt%), the
   Al–Fe eutectics (Fe cap 0.5 wt%), and Addalloy-type Al–4.5Mg–1.5Zr (Zr cap 1 wt%). Its
   Mg + Si ≤ 6 wt% joint cap even excludes AlSi10Mg. Settle these at the design-space freeze

    (a.out / "runs.json").write_text(json.dumps(rows, indent=0) + "\n")
    write_summaries(rows, a.out)


def write_summaries(rows, out):
    summary = summarize(rows)
    with open(out / "summary.csv", "w", newline="") as fh:
        w = csv.DictWriter(fh, fieldnames=list(summary[0]))
        w.writeheader()
        w.writerows({k: (round(v, 4) if isinstance(v, float) else v) for k, v in s.items()} for s in summary)
    diffs = paired(rows)
    with open(out / "paired_vs_333.csv", "w", newline="") as fh:
        w = csv.DictWriter(fh, fieldnames=list(diffs[0]))
        w.writeheader()
        w.writerows({k: (round(v, 4) if isinstance(v, float) else v) for k, v in d.items()} for d in diffs)
    for sc in SCENARIOS:
        print(f"\n{sc}: mean best of 25 (+/- 1 se), best after 12, P(beat best baseline by 0.05), P(found the better bump)")
        for s in summary:
            if s["scenario"] == sc:
                print(f"  {s['split']:<22} {s['mean_best']:.3f} +/- {s['se_best']:.3f}   {s['mean_best_at_12']:.3f}"
                      f"   {s['p_beat_baseline']:.2f}   {s['p_better_bump']:.2f}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

[Appended Cell #2] [stdout]
# Seeding the BOFN campaign: which experiments come first (#275)

[#275](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/275) asks how to choose the
initial experiments for the Al alloy campaign in
[#255](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/255), which
[#256](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/256) schedules. It suggests
a mix of three sources, about three runs each:

- **agent-chosen** compositions (literature, databases, CALPHAD);
- **known baselines** (AlSi10Mg, Scalmalloy);
- **Sobol** or another space-filling design.

It also asks:

- how to bring in the databases from [#7](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/7)
  and [#8](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/8);
- how "fantasy" data (synthetic, or from the literature) could stand in until real data exist;
- whether 3 + 3 + 3 makes sense with 25 experiments left.

Edison Scientific was the rubber duck: two `LITERATURE_HIGH` reviews and a critique of this
draft. They're in [`edison/`](edison/).

**Status:** this is a plan. Nothing here has been run on a real sample. The compositions are
proposals. They still need the CALPHAD screen, the design-space freeze, and a check of what is
actually on the shelf.

## Short answers

**On 3 + 3 + 3 with 25 left:** keep the three-way mix, but use about 6–7 seeds rather than 9. Give
the runs this frees up to the optimizer.

- **Edison's verdict on 9 seeds is "slightly too many".** Nine seeds are 36 % of the 25 runs.
  Bossek et al. (2020, [10.1145/3377930.3390155](https://doi.org/10.1145/3377930.3390155)) found
  that an initial design of about 30 % of the budget did best on their benchmark suite. Edison
  suggests 3 baselines, 2 agent picks, 2 space-filling points, 14 optimizer runs and 4 finalist
  runs ([q1](edison/q1-seeding-strategy/artifact-00.md)).
- **A toy simulation agrees on the direction** ([below](#how-many-seeds-a-toy-check)). Across 60
  paired problem instances, 2 baselines + 3 agent + 1 space-filling beat 3 + 3 + 3 by
  0.043 ± 0.014 in the best value found. It beat the best baseline 75 % of the time, against
  55 % for 3 + 3 + 3. 3 + 3 + 3 did worst of all the optimizer splits when the agent picks only
  pointed back at the known alloy family. That is the circularity risk Edison also flags.
- **Don't add a third baseline run.** The 6063 runs (A1–A5) and commercial AlSi10Mg powder at P1
  are baselines that cost no design run. D1-r stays: it measures the benchmark's own spread
  ([#256](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/blob/claude/issue-256-20261112-2149/al-campaign-schedule/README.md#the-36-al-runs)).

**In the schedule's terms** ([table](#a-proposed-seed-set)):

- D1 and D2 are the baselines.
- S1–S2 are agent picks, with different strengthening mechanisms.
- S3–S4 are space-filling picks from [`seed_design.py`](seed_design.py), made after the CALPHAD
  screen trims the candidate pool.
- B30 stays a dosing check. B15 should check the element the agent picks depend on (Mn, or Zr)
  rather than Si a second time.
- If the flex slots X1–X3 (Dec 14–16) aren't needed to redo failed runs, use them as early
  optimizer picks, not as more seeds.

**What matters more than the split:**

1. **The optimizer picks R1 (Dec 18) and R2 (Jan 8) before any new composition has strength
   data.** Seed tensile bars print at P3 (Jan 12–13). Until then, the strength nodes run on
   priors. So the literature data and strength models that go into those priors decide the first
   six optimizer runs ([pseudo-data](#literature-and-fantasy-data)).
2. **Most of the literature's best Sc-free seeds need Zr, Fe, Ce or Cu.** None of these is on
   the Nov 13 list in [#146](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/146#issuecomment-6842840090)
   (Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Mg, Sc, Er, Ti from ESPI; Si, Fe, Ni and Cu were never ordered). The
   Scalmalloy-type benchmark D2 needs Zr as well. Check whether Zr is coming. If not, order it as
   an Al–Zr master alloy before the S runs (Dec 7–10).
3. **The design box on [PR #72](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/pull/72)
   excludes several of the best-documented Sc-free LPBF alloys:** Al–10Ce (Ce cap 6 wt%), the
   Al–Fe eutectics (Fe cap 0.5 wt%), and Addalloy-type Al–4.5Mg–1.5Zr (Zr cap 1 wt%). Its
   Mg + Si ≤ 6 wt% joint cap even excludes AlSi10Mg. Settle these at the design-space freeze
   (G0, today).
4. **Settle the mineral-burden metric before picking seeds.** Of the 15 palette elements, only
   Fe, Si and Cu are absent from the USGS 2022 critical minerals list. By a plain wt% count of
   listed elements, Al–4Mn–0.5Ti–0.5Zr (5 wt%) is only a little leaner than Scalmalloy (about
   6 wt%, counting Mg). It wins clearly only if the metric weights Sc's supply risk well above
   Mn's. Fe- and
   Si-based strengthening is where "stronger and leaner" is easiest to show.

**Space-filling:** use the integr
<...output truncated to 10000 characters (edit the cell to produce a shorter output if needed)...>

- **Strength:**
  - review tables: Aversa et al. 2019, [10.3390/ma12071007](https://doi.org/10.3390/ma12071007),
    and Liu et al. 2024, [10.1088/2631-7990/ad1657](https://doi.org/10.1088/2631-7990/ad1657);
  - the Luo 2024 AlSi10Mg process-structure-property set on Zenodo, listed in
    [`alloy-databases.md`](../alloy-databases.md);
  - an AlSi10Mg tensile set (Jatti et al., PLOS ONE, [10.1371/journal.pone.0324049](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0324049)).
- **Wrought and cast handbook data only:**
  - Knovel, Total Materia and MatWeb. These give the wrought 6063 baseline, not LPBF behaviour.
- **No use at these nodes:**
  - the DFT repositories (AFLOW, OQMD, JARVIS, NOMAD).

Edison couldn't verify the DOI it gave for a separate Barrionuevo AlSi10Mg data descriptor, so
check that DOI before using it.

## Making the seeds count for the paper

The schedule pre-registers an AI benchmark at G1 (Dec 4). Edison q1 (§6, P9) makes three points
about it:

- **Use one common seed set for every policy:** random, expert design of experiments, standard
  BO and BOFN. That set is the baselines and the space-filling seeds.
- **Count the agent picks on purpose.** Either put them in the common set, or charge them to the
  AI policy's budget. Report the warm-start effect and the optimizer's effect separately.
- **Replay only on points that were actually measured.** Anything else needs a clearly labelled,
  cross-validated simulator, and causal acceleration claims should be avoided.

With about 20 compositions, the acceleration factor will rest on that simulator. Space-filling
seeds make the simulator less wrong away from the optimizer's path. That is one more reason to
keep one or two of them.

## Pitfalls

From Edison q1's table ([artifact-01](edison/q1-seeding-strategy/artifact-01.md)) and this work:

| Pitfall | Do instead |
|---|---|
| Nine seeds leave only 12 optimizer runs | About 6–7 seeds |
| A 10d rule would need 140–150 runs in 15-D | Shrink the space before atomizing: at most 3–4 additions, CALPHAD descriptors as GP inputs, sparse kernels |
| Agent picks cluster around Al–Si–Mg and Al–Mg–Sc–Zr | Two picks, with different mechanisms and element sets, chosen away from D1 and D2 |
| Sobol in the full 15-element simplex is almost never feasible | Sample face by face on the sparse simplex (as `seed_design.py` does) |
| Maximin picks extreme corners | `imse`, or maximin only after the CALPHAD screen trims the pool |
| Euclidean distance ignores element identity | Add an element-set term (`--set-weight`) |
| Composition-only space-filling leaves the downstream nodes cold | Seed each node from its own cheap sources; space-fill in descriptor and print-parameter space |
| Pseudo-data pooled with real data biases the model | A source column, per-source noise, multi-task or multi-fidelity; never overwrite rows |
| Seeds differ between the compared policies | One common seed set; report warm-start and optimizer effects separately |
| The seeds need elements we don't have | Check Zr, Fe and Ce now; B15 checks the element the S picks depend on |
| Failed runs dropped from the data | Record failures as outcomes ([#274](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/274)) |

## Files

| File | What |
|---|---|
| [`seeds.csv`](seeds.csv) | Points already chosen: 6063, D1, D2, B30, B15. Add the agent picks here, and replace nominal compositions with measured ones as they come in |
| [`seed_design.py`](seed_design.py) | Space-filling picks around `seeds.csv`, in composition space or, after the CALPHAD screen, in descriptor space |
| [`budget_split_sim.py`](budget_split_sim.py) | The toy simulation of seed and optimizer splits of 25 runs |
| [`results/`](results/) | Outputs of both scripts |
| [`edison/`](edison/) | The Edison queries, answers, artifacts and full trajectories, plus `edison_tasks.py`, which submits, waits for and fetches them |

```bash
pip install numpy scipy
python bofn-seeding/seed_design.py                       # 3 picks, imse
python bofn-seeding/seed_design.py --compare             # all four methods
python bofn-seeding/seed_design.py --elements Mn Cr Mg Si Er Ti Zn Zr   # once Zr is on the shelf
python bofn-seeding/seed_design.py --candidates screen.csv --features freezing_range kou_index l12_fraction

pip install torch botorch
python bofn-seeding/budget_split_sim.py --reps 30 --workers 4   # about 10 min on 4 cores
```

| q1: rubber-duck the 3 + 3 + 3 plan | `LITERATURE_HIGH` | `2d0326f1-fc13-4a90-bcd0-6f92d885d5c8` | [`edison/q1-seeding-strategy/`](edison/q1-seeding-strategy/) |

the papers, so check a value against its source before it goes into a prior.

258: ## How many seeds: a toy check

260: [`budget_split_sim.py`](budget_split_sim.py) is a flat-GP toy, not a model of the campaign:
261: 
262: - **The space.** A 6-D unit box, where the response depends mostly on 3 hidden dimensions.
263: - **The response.** A "known family" bump of height 0.7, where the baselines sit (good, not
264:   best). A better bump of height 1.0 somewhere else, and a decoy.
265: - **The seeds.** The agent picks are drawn around the better bump ("agent right") or around the
266:   known family ("agent wrong"). One free weak point stands in for 6063.
267: - **The optimizer.** The remaining runs go to batches of 3, picked by qLogEI.
268: - **The runs.** 30 problem instances per scenario. Every split sees the same instances, so the
269:   differences are paired.

1: #!/usr/bin/env python3
2: """Pick space-filling seed compositions around the points already chosen (#275).
3: 
4: #275 suggests taking Sobol points but throwing out the ones that land too close to existing
5: experiments. This script does that, plus two more model-based variants, in the space a GP
6: with a ``Normalize`` input transform over the design box would see (each element's wt%
7: divided by its upper bound), plus ``--set-weight`` (default 0.5) for every element that one
8: alloy has and the other doesn't, so different element sets count as further apart:
9: 
10: - ``sobol``: the first n feasible points of a scrambled Sobol sequence. Ignores the existing
11:   points; this is the plain baseline.
12: - ``sobol-exclusion``: walk the same Sobol sequence and skip any point closer than ``--radius``
13:   to an existing or already-picked point (the heuristic in #275).
14: - ``maximin``: greedy maximin augmentation over a large Sobol candidate pool. Each pick is the
15:   candidate farthest from its nearest existing or picked point.
16: - ``imse`` (default): greedy integrated-variance reduction. Each pick is the candidate that most
17:   lowers the average posterior variance of a GP (RBF kernel, fixed length scale) over the whole
18:   feasible pool, given the existing and picked points. Before any outcome is measured the GP
19:   variance depends only on where the points are, so this needs no data. Unlike maximin it
20:   doesn't push every pick into a corner of the box.
21: 
22: The design space follows the finalized element bounds on PR #72 (Edison task ``caec5419``):
23: Al balance at least 85 wt%, the recommended upper bound per element, a 0.10 wt% floor for any
24: element that is switched on, and the joint caps (Mn+Cr <= 7, Sc+Zr <= 1.5, Cu+Mg <= 5,
25: Cu+Li <= 4, Mg+Zn+Li <= 10 wt%). Mg+Si <= 6 is left out on purpose, because AlSi10Mg, the
26: benchmark, breaks it. Each candidate has at most ``--k-max`` additions (sparse sub-systems)
27: and at least ``--min-total`` wt% of additions in all (default 3; 6063 has about 1, the
28: Scalmalloy-type benchmark about 6, AlSi10Mg about 10).
29: 
30: Existing points come from ``seeds.csv`` (baselines, dosing checks, agent picks; use measured
31: compositions once there are any). The default element set is what is on hand or shipping per
32: #146 on 2026-11-13: Mn, Cr, Mg, Ti, Er and Zn from ESPI, plus Si through 4047 powder. Sn (cap
33: 0.1 wt%) and Sc (the mineral the campaign is trying to avoid; D2 already covers it) are left
34: out. Add Zr with ``--elements ... Zr`` once it is on the shelf.

1: #!/usr/bin/env python3
2: """Toy check of how to split 25 design runs between seeds and optimizer rounds (#275).
3: 
4: This is a deliberately small, flat-GP simulation. It is not a model of the alloy campaign; it
5: only asks how the split behaves under assumptions we can state:
6: 
7: - 6-D unit box (a normalized composition space). The response depends mostly on 3 hidden
8:   "active" dimensions, like an alloy whose strength is driven by a few additions.
9: - A "known family" bump of height 0.7 where the baselines sit (AlSi10Mg-like: good, not best),
10:   a better bump of height 1.0 somewhere else, and a smaller decoy. Observation noise sd 0.02.
11: - One free weak point (the 6063 A-block runs), which doesn't count toward the 25.
12: - Baseline seeds sit in the known-family bump. Agent seeds are drawn around a guess with
13:   sd 0.2 in the active dimensions. The guess is the better bump ("agent right") or the known
14:   family ("agent wrong": the literature points back at what is already known).
15: - Space-filling seeds are scrambled Sobol points. The remaining runs go to batches of 3
16:   picked by qLogEI over a 2048-point Sobol candidate set (the last batch may be smaller).
17: 
18: Every split is run on the same problem instances (same seeds), so differences are paired.
19: 
20:     python bofn-seeding/budget_split_sim.py --reps 30 --workers 4
21: """

Skill directory: /workspace/.skills/citation-integrity

- Always cite sources for claims, either to a primary source or a subagent task.
- Every primary source needs a full BibTeX entry. Cite from the BibTeX, not from a narrative answer.
- Never cite yourself or guess citations from memory.

## Web sources

Every source you use from the `e14c.web` tools needs a full BibTeX entry.

- When you write an entry yourself, name its key with the first author's surname, the year, and the first word of the title, for example `jumper2021highly`. This keeps keys unique.
- Save each entry with `e14c.web.save_citation(bibtex)` as soon as you use the source. It appends the entry to your own file in the project's citations folder, `$WORKSPACE_PATH/citations/$PROJECT_ID/$TRAJECTORY_ID.bib`. In a chat session, `TRAJECTORY_ID` is the session ID. Do not write citation files any other way.

### Sources with a DOI

Call `await e14c.web.cite_doi(doi)`. It fetches the BibTeX from doi.org and saves it. This works for Crossref and DataCite DOIs, including arXiv DOIs such as `10.48550/arXiv.1706.03762`. Check that the title and authors in the returned entry match the paper you read.

### Sources without a DOI

Write the BibTeX entry yourself. Take every field from the source, never from memory.

- Use `@online` for web pages, database records, datasets, software, and reports. The report template hides URLs for most entry types, but it always prints them for `@online`, so readers can find the source.
- Include `author`, `title`, `url`, and `urldate`. `urldate` is the date you accessed the page, written as `YYYY-MM-DD`. Add `date` when the page shows a publication or update date.
- When there is no personal author, put the organization in `author` inside double braces, such as `{{UniProt Consortium}}`. The double braces stop it from being split into first and last names. Use the organization's short name in the key.
- When the page has no date, use the access year in the key.
- Many scholarly pages list their title, authors, and date in `citation_*` meta tags. `(await e14c.web.fetch_page(url)).text` returns the raw HTML so you can read them.
- In `title`, escape `&`, `%`, `_`, and `#` with a backslash, and wrap acronyms in braces to keep their capitals. Do not escape anything in `url`.
- For a journal article with no DOI, use `@article` with `journal`, `volume`, `number`, `pages`, and `year` instead. These fields let a reader find it without a link.

```bibtex
@online{uniprot2026uniprotkb,
  author  = {{UniProt Consortium}},
  title   = {{UniProtKB} entry {P04637} ({P53\_HUMAN}): Cellular tumor antigen p53},
  url     = {https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P04637/entry},
  urldate = {2026-10-12},
}
```

def optimize_acqf_discrete(
    acq_function: AcquisitionFunction,
    q: int,
    choices: Tensor,
    max_batch_size: int = 2048,
    unique: bool = True,
    return_acq_values: bool = True,
    X_avoid: Tensor | None = None,
    inequality_constraints: list[tuple[Tensor, Tensor, float]] | None = None,
) -> tuple[Tensor, Tensor]:
    r"""Optimize over a discrete set of points using batch evaluation.

    For ``q > 1`` this function generates candidates by means of sequential
    conditioning (rather than joint optimization), since for all but the
    smalles number of choices the set ``choices^q`` of discrete points to
    evaluate quickly explodes.

    Args:
        acq_function: An AcquisitionFunction.
        q: The number of candidates.
        choices: A ``num_choices x d`` tensor of possible choices.
        max_batch_size: The maximum number of choices to evaluate in batch.
            A large limit can cause excessive memory usage if the model has
            a large training set.
        unique: If True return unique choices, o/w choices may be repeated
            (only relevant if ``q > 1``).
        X_avoid: An ``n x d`` tensor of candidates that we aren't allowed to pick.
            These will be removed from the set of choices.
        inequality constraints: A list of tuples (indices, coefficients, rhs),
            with each tuple encoding an inequality constraint of the form
            ``\sum_i (X[indices[i]] * coefficients[i]) >= rhs``.
            Infeasible points will be removed from the set of choices.
        return_acq_values: Return acquisition values.
            Can be set to False to avoid memory
            intensive joint forward evaluation of the acquisition function.

    Returns:
        A two-element tuple containing

        - a ``q x d``-dim tensor of generated candidates.
        - an associated acquisition value.
    """
    if isinstance(acq_function, OneShotAcquisitionFunction):
        raise UnsupportedError(
            "Discrete optimization is not supported for one-shot acquisition functions."
        )
    if X_avoid is not None and unique:
        choices = _filter_invalid(X=choices, X_avoid=X_avoid)
    if inequality_constraints is not None:
        choices = _filter_infeasible(
            X=choices, inequality_constraints=inequality_constraints
        )
    len_choices = len(choices)
    if len_choices == 0:
        message = "`choices` must be non-empty."
        if X_avoid is not None or inequality_constraints is not None:
            message += (
                " No feasible points remain after removing `X_avoid` and "
                "filtering out infeasible points."
            )
        raise InputDataError(message)
    elif len_choices < q and unique:
        warnings.warn(
            (
                f"Requested {q=} candidates from fully discrete search "
                f"space, but only {len_choices} possible choices remain. "
            ),
            OptimizationWarning,
            stacklevel=2,
        )
        q = len_choices
    choices_batched = choices.unsqueeze(-2)
    if q > 1:
        candidate_list, acq_value_list = [], []
        base_X_pending = acq_function.X_pending
        for _ in range(q):
            with torch.no_grad():
                acq_values = _split_batch_eval_acqf(
                    acq_function=acq_function,
                    X=choices_batched,
                    max_batch_size=max_batch_size,
                )
            best_idx = torch.argmax(acq_values)
            candidate_list.append(choices_batched[best_idx])
            acq_value_list.append(acq_values[best_idx])
            # set pending points
            candidates = torch.cat(candidate_list, dim=-2)
            acq_function.set_X_pending(
                torch.cat([base_X_pending, candidates], dim=-2)
                if base_X_pending is not None
                else candidates
            )
            # need to remove choice from choice set if enforcing uniqueness
            if unique:
                choices_batched = torch.cat(
                    [choices_batched[:best_idx], choices_batched[best_idx + 1 :]]
                )

        # Reset acq_func to previous X_pending state
        acq_function.set_X_pending(base_X_pending)
        best_acq_values = torch.stack(acq_value_list)

    else:
        with torch.no_grad():
            acq_values = _split_batch_eval_acqf(
                acq_function=acq_function,
                X=choices_batched,
                max_batch_size=max_batch_size,
            )
        best_idx = torch.argmax(acq_values)
        candidates = choices_batched[best_idx]
        best_acq_values = acq_values[best_idx]

    if not return_acq_values:
        return candidates, None
    return candidates, best_acq_values

## Abstract

The expansion of the material library for the laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process is essential for the further establishment of the process in areas such as the aerospace and automotive industries. In this study, we designed a high-strength and low-cost Al-Mn-Ti-Zr alloy specifically tailored to the unique conditions of the LPBF process. Gas-atomized pre-alloyed powder was prepared and used as feedstock to fabricate LPBF specimens for microstructural examination and mechanical testing. By taking advantage of the high solidification rate, unconventionally large amounts of Mn (3.7 ± 0.5 wt%) are metastably frozen within the α-Al matrix, contributing significantly to solid solution hardening (~104 MPa ≙ 37% share of yield strength). The as-built specimens exhibit a yield strength of 284 ± 3 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength of 320 ± 1 MPa, and an elongation at fracture of 16.9 ± 0.2%. This new alloy exhibits a bimodal microstructure consisting of alternately distributed fine equiaxed and coarse columnar grain regions. Further microstructural analyses reveal a high number of primary L12 cubic Al3(Tix Zr1 - x) nanoparticles within the equiaxed α-Al grains near the bottom of the melt pool. A highly coherent interface with the α-Al matrix confirms high efficiency for heterogeneous nucleation during solidification. In addition to the Al3(Tix Zr1 - x) nanoparticles, an AlxMn(Fe, Si) phase with a quasi-crystalline structure is observed along the grain boundaries and interdendritic areas.

## 1. Introduction

Sequential Model-Based Optimization (SMBO) algorithms are techniques for the optimization of problems for which the evaluation of solution candidates is resource-intensive, such as problems requiring real physical experiments or problems that require computationally-expensive simulations. The latter are particularly present in almost any application of Artificial Intelligence, most notably in terms of parameter tuning problems – a problem that is also omnipresent in Evolutionary Computation (Lobo et al., 2007). SMBO-based techniques are among the most successfully applied hyper-parameter tuning methods (Hutter et al., 2011; Bartz-Beielstein, 2010; Falkner et al., 2018; Kotthoff et al., 2019), so that research on this family of iterative optimization heuristics has gained significant traction in the last decade. SMBO forms today an integral part of the state-of-the-art heuristic solvers. Its probably best-known representatives are Bayesian Optimization (see surveys by (Shahriari et al., 2016; Mockus, 1989; Rasmussen and Williams, 2006)) and, in particular, Efficient Global Optimization (EGO, (Jones et al., 1998)).

The generic SMBO method works as follows. An initial design of points is sampled and evaluated with the true objective function. The eponymous sequential part iteratively (1) builds a surrogate of the true objective function (on basis of the already evaluated samples), (2) proposes new samples by optimizing a so-called infill-criterion (which is sometimes referred to as acquisition function), (3) evaluates these additional samples, and (4) integrates these samples, together with their quality indicators (“function values”, “fitness”) into the memory. Each of these steps offers a great variety of design choices, which all may affect the performance of the SMBO procedure. Which surrogate model should be used? Which of the countless infill criteria to use? What method should be used to create the initial sample and what proportion of the overall budget should be spent on the initial design? While a large body of works addresses the first two questions (see surveys mentioned above), the latter two questions are treated rather poorly. In this work we aim to shed light on the relevance of a suitably chosen initial sampling strategy. More precisely, we study how the size of the initial design and the strategy used to generate it affects the performance of SMBO. As a well-established benchmark environment offering a great variety of different numerical optimization problems, we chose the 24 noiseless BBOB functions (in different dimensions) as test-bed for our investigation.

## Abstract

Conventional precipitation-hardened aluminum alloys experience severe mechanical degradation above 200 °C due to precipitate coarsening and dissolution. This study presents a novel Al–Fe-Mg Zr eutectic alloy fabricated via laser powder bed fusion, achieving crack-free fabrication with 99.8% relative density, ultrafine grains, and a heterogeneous cellular-lamellar microstructure. Direct aging (400 °C/4 h) enhances yield strength (YS) to 376.1 MPa (72.6% increase) and ultimate tensile strength to 405.8 MPa (30.7% increase) compared to the as-printed condition, while reducing ductility to 11.1%. The strengthening mechanisms arise from grain boundary strengthening, precipitation strengthening via coherent L12-Al3Zr nanoscale dispersoids, dislocation strengthening, and effective load transfer through submicron-scale Al–Fe intermetallic phases. High-temperature tensile testing reveals excellent mechanical stability, retaining a YS of 124 MPa at 350 °C. After prolonged thermal exposure (400 °C/100 h), the alloy maintains good mechanical properties, demonstrating excellent heat resistance due to the low coarsening rate of Al13Fe4 (0.98 nm 3/s) and sustained Al3Zr precipitates. The dual-scale strengthening strategy significantly advances developing high-strength and thermally stable Al alloys for high performance applications.

This study presents a novel Al–Fe-Mg Zr eutectic alloy fabricated via laser powder bed fusion, achieving crack-free fabrication with 99.8% relative density, ultrafine grains, and a heterogeneous cellular-lamellar microstructure. Direct aging (400 °C/4 h) enhances yield strength (YS) to 376.1 MPa (72.6% increase) and ultimate tensile strength to 405.8 MPa (30.7% increase) compared to the as-printed condition, while reducing ductility to 11.1%. The strengthening mechanisms arise from grain boundary strengthening, precipitation strengthening via coherent L12-Al3Zr nanoscale dispersoids, dislocation strengthening, and effective load transfer through submicron-scale Al–Fe intermetallic phases. After prolonged thermal exposure (400 °C/100 h), the alloy maintains good mechanical properties, demonstrating excellent heat resistance due to the low coarsening rate of Al13Fe4 (0.98 nm 3/s) and sustained Al3Zr precipitates. The dual-scale strengthening strategy significantly advances developing high-strength and thermally stable Al alloys for high performance applications.

Authors:

## Abstract

Sequential model-based optimization (SMBO) approaches are algorithms for solving problems that require computationally or otherwise expensive function evaluations. The key design principle of SMBO is a substitution of the true objective function by a surrogate, which is used to propose the point(s) to be evaluated next.

SMBO algorithms are intrinsically modular, leaving the user with many important design choices. Significant research efforts go into understanding which settings perform best for which type of problems. Most works, however, focus on the choice of the model, the acquisition function, and the strategy used to optimize the latter. The choice of the initial sampling strategy, however, receives much less attention. Not surprisingly, quite diverging recommendations can be found in the literature.

We analyze in this work how the size and the distribution of the initial sample influences the overall quality of the efficient global optimization (EGO) algorithm, a well-known SMBO approach. While, overall, small initial budgets using Halton sampling seem preferable, we also observe that the performance landscape is rather unstructured. We furthermore identify several situations in which EGO performs unfavorably against random sampling. Both observations indicate that an adaptive SMBO design could be beneficial, making SMBO an interesting test-bed for automated algorithm design.

    """
    Extract a PDF, notebook, DOCX, or PPTX into files and return their directory.

    from e14c.read import read, view_image

# Effect of thermomechanical processing on mechanical properties and the microstructure of ternary Al-Ce-Mg alloy

- …
- Catalin R. Picu 1 

## Abstract

Al-Ce alloys are known to retain a large fraction of their room temperature properties at elevated temperatures and after exposure to temperature for extended periods. Here we work with the ternary close-to-eutectic alloy Al-10Ce-4Mg and explore the effect of extrusion on its microstructure and mechanical properties. Extrusion produces a highly refined microstructure with texture exhibiting a twofold increase in strength (tensile strength of 390 MPa at room temperature) and fourfold increase in failure strain relative to the as cast state. After exposure to 300 °C for 100 h the alloy retains 82% and 88% of the room temperature strength in the as-cast and extruded states, respectively. The ratio of the strength at 300 °C to the strength at room temperature is 0.4, below the corresponding ratio for the Al-10Ce binary alloy (ratio 0.7) but higher than that of AA2618 (ratio 0.1). The extruded Al-10Ce-4Mg has fracture toughness of 23 kJ/m 2, which is retained in proportion of 97.6% after exposure to 300 °C for 100 h. The material exhibits negative strain rate sensitivity at room temperature and in the range of strain rates \(\:{10}^{-5}\:{s}^{-1}\) to \(\:{10}^{-2}\:{s}^{-1}\). We show that the high room temperature strength is due to Al 11 Ce 3 dispersoids and Mg-rich precipitates. The Mg-rich precipitates dissolve in the temperature range 200 °C to 250 °C while the Al 11 Ce 3 dispersoids remain stable and provide strengthening at 300 °C. Mg-rich precipitates reform upon cooling, which ensures property retention upon thermal cycling. The high toughness, strength and property retention upon exposure to elevated temperatures make this alloy an excellent candidate for applications requiring lightweight temperature resistant materials.

## Introduction

A need exists for light materials with enhanced thermal stability to be used in supersonic aircraft design. The use of Al alloys would provide higher fuel savings, lower CO 2 emissions, and overall increased energy efficiency. However, the use of current Al alloys from the AA2XXX and AA7XXX class, which are precipitate hardened, is impossible as their properties degrade above ~ 200\(\:℃\) due to the dissolution and/or coarsening of precipitates(Gao et al. 2019)(Mondol et al. 2017). In contrast, the Al-Ce intermetallics are highly stable and resist coarsening up to at least 350 °C (Guo et al. 2022, Shen et al. 2023, Nam et al. 2023, Singh et al. 2024). This drives the emergence of a new generation of castable Al-Ce alloys with significantly improved high-temperature strength (Shen et al. 2023, Stojanovic et al. 2018, Sims et al. 2016, El-Hadad et al. 2023, Weiss and Cerium 2019, Huda and Edi 2013).

Ce is a relatively abundant rare earth element (REE) which may be obtained as a byproduct of the extraction and purification of more valuable REEs, including Li, Pr, Nd, Dy, and Tb (Sims et al. 2022). Cerium lacks high-volume applications at present time (Weiss and Cerium 2019, Czerwinski 2019). When added to Al as an alloying element, Ce forms the Al 11 Ce 3 intermetallic, with an eutectic point at 10% Ce (Sims et al. 2017) (all percentages in wt%). Microstructures with off-eutectic compositions contain a dominant Al (fcc) phase for hypoeutectic, and script-like (or plate-shaped) Al 11 Ce 3 intermetallics in the case of hypereutectic alloys (Perrin et al. 2023, Okamoto 2011, Cao et al. 2017, Dai et al. 2023, Sun et al. 2019, Kozakevich et al. 2023, Ye et al. 2023, Rogachev and Naumova 2021). The non-uniform distribution of the intermetallics in the as-cast state leads to sub-optimal strengthening. Nevertheless, Al-Ce alloys in the near-eutectic range (5–15% Ce) exhibit excellent castability and resistance to hot tearing and cracking (Plotkowski et al. 2020).

Effect of precipitation-forming elements in a near-eutectic Al-Ce alloy for Laser Powder Bed Fusion https://doi.org/10.1016/j.addma.2022.102959
# Effect of precipitation-forming elements in a near-eutectic Al-Ce alloy for Laser Powder Bed Fusion

Additive manufacturing. Published: 2022-06-10. 23 citations.

## Abstract

Despite a growing interest in additive manufacturing technologies, there is still a limited selection of suitable materials developed regarding the unique non-equilibrium cooling conditions. A highly promising alloy system for Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) is Al-Ce, which shows outstanding processability in recent studies. The medium strengths already achievable with the binary system are to be improved in these investigations by additional precipitation-forming elements. By adding Mg and Si, a very high tensile strength of 593 MPa in the as-built condition can be achieved. XRD measurements show that the addition of these two elements lead to additional formation of an AlCeSi phase and phases of the Mg2Si precipitation sequence, which affects the usually expected eutectic formation of the Al11Ce3 phase. Contrary to the expected dominance of the binary intermetallics, AlCeSi in particular can be identified. The Al11Ce3 content in the microstructure can only be significantly increased with modified parameter combinations or volume energy inputs. Along with this, additional differences in grain size and grain morphology can be identified by EBSD investigations. The influence of the parameters extend to different mechanical properties as a function of the applied parameter combinations. With the very good additive processability in the form of wide process parameter windows, the parameter combinations can be used to adjust the properties in the as-built state.

## 7\. Conclusions

In this paper we have presented a database for data-driven investigations of the sequential model-based optimization (SMBO) strategy EGO *([Jones et al., 1998](https://arxiv.org/html/2003.13826#bib.bib31))*. The focus of our work is on analyzing the influence of the (size and type of) initial design on the overall performance of EGO. Our data base contains data for 720 different problems, which are evaluated against a total of 40 different initial design strategies.

While we clearly observed that small initial designs are preferable at a high-level view, we also found that each of the 40 considered combinations of design type and size achieved best performance on at least one of the 720 problems. Our findings thus confirm that an automated strategy selection method – like the proof-of-concept approach presented in *([Saini et al., 2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2003.13826#bib.bib48))* – might indeed be profitable. Moreover, we even identified cases in which the usage of EGO does not provide any benefits over the initial (quasi-)random sample – especially in case of highly multimodal problems.

Our long-term vision are SMBO approaches that dynamically decide whether to take the next sample from a (quasi-)random distribution or whether to derive it from the surrogate model. Going one step further, we believe that an adaptive choice of the acquisition function, and possibly even of the solver used to optimize the latter, should bring substantial performance gains – in particular in the case in which the total budget is known in advance. Hence, we need to “train” a final recommendation (last evaluation) instead of achieving good anytime performance. These two mentioned questions fall under the umbrella of dynamic algorithm configuration, which has been an important driver for the field of evolutionary computation for the last decades *([Burke et al., 2013](https://arxiv.org/html/2003.13826#bib.bib13); [Eiben et al., 1999](https://arxiv.org/html/2003.13826#bib.bib18); [Karafotias et al., 2015](https://arxiv.org/html/2003.13826#bib.bib32); [Doerr and Doerr, 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2003.13826#bib.bib17))*, and which has recently also gained interest in machine learning communities *([Biedenkapp et al., 2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2003.13826#bib.bib6))*.

Typically, the budget of common SMBO applications is too small for a classical a priori (i.e., offline) landscape-aware selection of the optimizer design based on supervised learning approaches (see *([Kerschke et al., 2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2003.13826#bib.bib33))* for a survey). However, in case high-level properties – such as the degree of (multi-)modality or the sizes of the problem’s attraction basins – are known for the problem at hand, or can be guessed by an expert, selecting a suitable initial design strategy is feasible.

Finally, we have seen that the performance of the different designs was often quite comparable. To investigate the differences in more detail, we suggest to consider the different strategies as a portfolio of different algorithms. With this viewpoint, one could analyze the marginal contributions *([Xu et al., 2012](https://arxiv.org/html/2003.13826#bib.bib52))* or Shapley values *([Fréchette et al., 2016](https://arxiv.org/html/2003.13826#bib.bib21))* of the different designs, and leverage the information contained therein.

{"code": "answer = r'''## Bottom line

I would retain the mixed seed strategy and a **provisional 6–7-seed target**, but the draft does not yet justify either that exact count or a general IMSE-over-maximin recommendation. Its strongest point is the warning about delayed strength feedback.

## 1. Corrections to the draft

- **“[Bossek et al.] found that an initial design of about 30 % of the budget did best on their benchmark suite.”** Replace with: “They generally favored small initial designs, with substantial problem dependence.” Their [conclusion](https://doi.org/10.1145/3377930.3390155) does not establish a general 30% optimum.
- **“Keep the three-way mix, but use about 6–7 seeds rather than 9.”** The proposed schedule still has **eight pre-optimizer runs**: D1, D2, B30, B15, S1–S4. Including D1-r and four finalist runs leaves exactly 12 optimizer runs. Identify which slot is removed/merged; relabeling dosing checks does not release budget. The toy instead gives *all* nonseed runs to optimization, without these reservations.
- **“Maximin sends every point to a corner.”** Change to “Maximin selected boundary-heavy points in this pool and metric.” Likewise, “hardest ... to melt, dose and print” is an untested feasibility judgment, not an output of the comparison.
- **“Each element one alloy has and the other doesn't adds 0.5 to the distance.”** It adds **0.25 to squared distance**. This distinction materially affects interpreting the exclusion radius.
- **“Exclusion starts to matter once the existing set is large: literature points, or a dense CALPHAD screen.”** A screen is a *candidate pool*, not observed coverage. Only genuinely available observations, with appropriate noise/fidelity, should count as existing information.

## 2. Code audit and executed checks

I reproduced `space_filling_compare.csv` to its reported precision and completed the full **30-replicate × two-scenario × eight-policy** budget rerun.

| Method | Mean nearest distance ↓ | Fill distance ↓ | Mean posterior variance ↓ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Sobol | 1.0290 | 1.8104 | 0.9277 |
| Maximin | 1.1056 | **1.7153** | 0.9548 |
| IMSE | **0.9550** | 1.7595 | **0.8950** |

**`seed_design.py`:**

- **Scaling is a modeling assumption.** Dividing by caps equates the full Ti range (0.5 wt%) with the full Si range (12 wt%). That is not automatically the campaign GP’s geometry: it assumes fixed bounds, equal length scales, and the additional presence features. Descriptor mode uses dataset-wide min–max scaling; freeze those bounds, handle correlated descriptors, and retain composition information where descriptors are insufficient.
- **The element-set term double-counts identity** relative to composition coordinates and jumps at *any* positive concentration. Trace impurities in measured compositions could switch every element “on.” Use a declared intentional-addition/detection threshold and test weights including zero. With weight 0.5, any different support already has distance ≥0.5: the default exclusion radius mostly tests same-support alloys. Seed-0’s pool actually contains **130 candidates** within radius 0.5 of existing points; exclusion is not intrinsically inactive, just inactive for the first selections.
- **The ≥3 wt% filter is unjustified as a strength screen.** It excludes lean precipitation-strengthened candidates—the goal includes reducing mineral burden. Remove it or demonstrate sensitivity. The reference measure also favors three-addition faces: 7,172 of 11,136 default candidates have three additions. “Average coverage” means coverage under this chosen face-sampling distribution, not uniform coverage of all plausible alloys.
- **IMSE algebra checks out** against direct posterior-variance reduction. But it assumes a noiseless, unit-amplitude radial-basis-function GP with fixed isotropic length scale 0.5. Treating *planned* seeds as noiseless observations is optimistic if they fail or remain unmeasured. Include observation noise and node-specific availability. My three-scramble checks retained IMSE’s average-coverage advantage at length scales 0.25, 0.5 and 1, and after removing the set penalty or total-addition cutoff; that is useful sensitivity evidence, not strength-performance validation.
- Rerun with **two** space-filling additions, changed B15, and actual S1/S2: the reported comparison uses three additions around the old five-row `seeds.csv`.

**`budget_split_sim.py`:**

- NumPy problems are paired, but **PyTorch acquisition sampling/fitting is not seeded**. My rerun gave 2+3+1 minus 3+3+3 = **+0.0479 ± 0.0164**, using one standard error across 30 problem clusters. Direction reproduced; exact supplied values did not. The two scenarios reuse the same 30 problems, so they are **not 60 independent instances**; cluster by problem when combining them.
- Baselines all cluster around **one** known bump—not distinct AlSi10Mg and Scalmalloy families. “Agent right” knows the optimum center and active dimensions; “wrong” merely revisits a good family, rather than proposing poor/unprintable alloys. This favors the claim that mistaken agents cost little.
- “Beat baseline” uses the best of **two versus three** baseline points, changing the threshold between policies. Use one fixed reference. “All 25 Sobol” is actually **two baselines + 23 Sobol**; rename it or implement the label.
- `unique=True` prevents duplication **within a batch only**. The pool is never depleted and previous observations are not excluded; my diagnostic found one cross-batch repeat. Explicitly permit/budget replication or exclude observed points. Log rather than suppress GP-fitting failures.
- Discrete-pool qLogEI is a reasonable **controlled flat-BO toy**, not a BOFN/p-KGFN surrogate. Seeds can lie off-pool; the optimizer cannot. Check larger pools or continuous optimization, noisy expected improvement, and especially delayed/partial feedback, feasibility and reserved confirmation runs. No seven-seed policy, IMSE seed policy, or maximin seed policy is tested here.

## 3. Is the disagreement resolved?

**Only conditionally.** IMSE wins the average-error criterion it targets; maximin wins the reported worst-case fill distance. Neither demonstrates better optimization. Boundary attraction is expected when maximizing separation, not an implementation bug.

I would prefer maximin when kernel length scales or reference-density weights are unreliable, when rare alloy families and worst-case coverage matter, or after a credible manufacturability screen removes unsafe extremes. A useful compromise is IMSE with a minimum-distance constraint, selected over a **physically reachable** pool. Do not let an equilibrium-only CALPHAD cutoff discard the supersaturated/metastable mechanisms being sought.

## 4. Proposed alloys and feedstock

**D1/D2 are sensible process-matched controls.** Commercial powder and wrought 6063 are valuable but cannot replace controls through the campaign’s own atomization/printing route. Keep B30 and an element-specific B15 only if they resolve separate, consequential dosing uncertainties.

**S1 is a defensible mechanism probe, not a demonstrated winner:** its [reported 284 MPa yield strength](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jallcom.2021.163156) overlaps the draft’s AlSi10Mg range and is below aged Scalmalloy. Its nucleation strategy also overlaps D2; Mn supersaturation is the important distinction.

**S2 needs a substantive correction.** The quoted **376 MPa yield strength** comes from [Li et al.](https://doi.org/10.1080/17452759.2025.2516663), whose measured printed alloy is **Al–1.87Fe–1.02Mg–1.03Zr**, not Al–(3–5)Fe–1Mg–(0.5–0.7)Zr. Those are different hypotheses. Use the documented chemistry or explicitly withdraw the property attribution. Al–10Ce is not automatically a better fallback: it violates the Ce cap, carries 10 wt% listed critical additions, and lacks a compelling room-temperature strength advantage as presented.

The Zr/Fe/Ce procurement warning is sound, but a purchase order is insufficient: establish delivery, carrier composition, dissolution time/temperature, recovery, and contamination. **Mass-balance the 6063 cups and master-alloy carriers**; nominally pure-Al candidates may be unreachable. Verify bulk chemistry, powder size/yield and oxygen before claiming literature transfer.

## 5. Prioritized changes before Dec 18

1. **Freeze success criteria:** yield versus ultimate strength, matched heat treatment/orientation, minimum ductility/density, and uncertainty-aware superiority. Define a dated mineral metric explicitly excluding/including Al; Sc-free is not synonymous with low burden.
2. **Fix the 25-run ledger and S2 attribution**, then commit to purchasable, reachable recipes. Consider a low-Sc bridge seed if matching aged Scalmalloy is central; zero-Sc and D2 alone weakly resolve that trade-off.
3. **Write a node-by-date data-availability contract.** Seed tensile results arrive Jan 19–22, not when bars print. Advance a sentinel tensile test if possible; otherwise label the first two batches as prior-driven for strength, while incorporating measured upstream evidence and pending evaluations.
4. **Freeze the executable optimization protocol:** objective, constraints, source-specific noise/fidelity, failures, pending points, repeats, and common seeds/budgets for policy comparisons. Dry-run the entire ingestion-to-batch pipeline.
5. **Rerun seed selection on the final screened pool**, with actual seeds, two additions, declared scaling/reference weights, and sensitivity checks—not the present default demonstration.

**Review choices:** I treated the attachments as the schedule authority; I clustered uncertainty by independent synthetic problem; I separated average prediction coverage from optimization performance and matched-condition strength claims.

## Making the seeds count for the paper

The schedule pre-registers an AI benchmark at G1 (Dec 4). Edison q1 (§6, P9) makes three points
about it:

  BO and BOFN. That set is the baselines and the space-filling seeds.
- **Count the agent picks on purpose.** Either put them in the common set, or charge them to the

- **Replay only on points that were actually measured.** Anything else needs a clearly labelled,

191: ## Space-filling around the points we already have
192: 
193: [`seed_design.py`](seed_design.py) adds space-filling points around everything in
194: [`seeds.csv`](seeds.csv): 6063, D1, D2, B30 and B15. Add the agent picks there.
195: 
196: **The space.** It is the box a GP with `Normalize` sees: each element's wt% divided by its upper
197: bound. On top of that, each element one alloy has and the other doesn't adds 0.5 to the distance,
198: so different element sets count as further apart. Edison flagged plain Euclidean distance for
199: sparse compositions (q1, P5).

203: - The bounds are the finalized ones on [PR #72](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/pull/72):
204:   Al ≥ 85 wt%, a cap per element, a 0.10 wt% floor for any element that is switched on, and its
205:   joint caps except Mg + Si.
206: - Each candidate has one to three additions, drawn from the elements on hand
207:   ([#146](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/146)): Mn, Cr, Mg, Ti, Er
208:   and Zn, plus Si through 4047.

251:   dense CALPHAD screen.

253:   cousin of the Al–Mn–Cr–Zr focus system. Use `imse`, but check its picks against the CALPHAD
254:   liquidus and cracking screen before dosing. Edison's objection to IMSE is that it needs a fitted
255:   GP. In fact it needs only kernel hyperparameters, but the length scale is a real choice. Rerun

258: ## How many seeds: a toy check

260: [`budget_split_sim.py`](budget_split_sim.py) is a flat-GP toy, not a model of the campaign:
261: 
262: - **The space.** A 6-D unit box, where the response depends mostly on 3 hidden dimensions.
263: - **The response.** A "known family" bump of height 0.7, where the baselines sit (good, not
264:   best). A better bump of height 1.0 somewhere else, and a decoy.
265: - **The seeds.** The agent picks are drawn around the better bump ("agent right") or around the
266:   known family ("agent wrong"). One free weak point stands in for 6063.
267: - **The optimizer.** The remaining runs go to batches of 3, picked by qLogEI.
268: - **The runs.** 30 problem instances per scenario. Every split sees the same instances, so the
269:   differences are paired.

271: | Split (baselines + agent + space-filling) | Seeds | Best of 25, agent right | Best of 25, agent wrong | Paired difference vs 3 + 3 + 3, both scenarios | P(beat best baseline by 0.05) |

288:   and spending all 25 runs on Sobol did worst.

290:   little when they don't.** They hurt mainly when they crowd the known family. 3 + 3 + 3 spends

292: - **2 + 3 + 1 was the most robust split.** It came near the top in both scenarios. 2 + 4 + 0 bets

136: def features(W, set_weight):
137:     """Normalized wt% plus set_weight x (element switched on): a mixed distance.
138: 
139:     Squared distance = range-scaled Euclidean + set_weight^2 x (number of elements in one alloy
140:     but not the other), so alloys with different element sets count as further apart (#275,
141:     Edison q1, pitfall P5).
142:     """
143:     return np.hstack([W / UB, set_weight * (W > 0)])

147: def _sqdist(A, B):
148:     return np.maximum((A * A).sum(1)[:, None] + (B * B).sum(1)[None, :] - 2 * A @ B.T, 0.0)

151: def _rbf(A, B, ell):
152:     return np.exp(-0.5 * _sqdist(A, B) / ell**2)

162:     for i, x in enumerate(Xc):

182:     """Prior-unit GP posterior variance at Xr given noise-free points Xd (locations only)."""

184:         return np.ones(len(Xr))

186:     V = np.linalg.solve(L, _rbf(Xd, Xr, ell))
187:     return np.clip(1.0 - (V * V).sum(0), 0.0, 1.0)

1: #!/usr/bin/env python3
2: """Pick space-filling seed compositions around the points already chosen (#275).
3: 
4: #275 suggests taking Sobol points but throwing out the ones that land too close to existing
5: experiments. This script does that, plus two more model-based variants, in the space a GP
6: with a ``Normalize`` input transform over the design box would see (each element's wt%
7: divided by its upper bound), plus ``--set-weight`` (default 0.5) for every element that one
8: alloy has and the other doesn't, so different element sets count as further apart:
9: 
10: - ``sobol``: the first n feasible points of a scrambled Sobol sequence. Ignores the existing
11:   points; this is the plain baseline.
12: - ``sobol-exclusion``: walk the same Sobol sequence and skip any point closer than ``--radius``
13:   to an existing or already-picked point (the heuristic in #275).
14: - ``maximin``: greedy maximin augmentation over a large Sobol candidate pool. Each pick is the
15:   candidate farthest from its nearest existing or picked point.
16: - ``imse`` (default): greedy integrated-variance reduction. Each pick is the candidate that most
17:   lowers the average posterior variance of a GP (RBF kernel, fixed length scale) over the whole
18:   feasible pool, given the existing and picked points. Before any outcome is measured the GP
19:   variance depends only on where the points are, so this needs no data. Unlike maximin it
20:   doesn't push every pick into a corner of the box.
21: 
22: The design space follows the finalized element bounds on PR #72 (Edison task ``caec5419``):
23: Al balance at least 85 wt%, the recommended upper bound per element, a 0.10 wt% floor for any
24: element that is switched on, and the joint caps (Mn+Cr <= 7, Sc+Zr <= 1.5, Cu+Mg <= 5,
25: Cu+Li <= 4, Mg+Zn+Li <= 10 wt%). Mg+Si <= 6 is left out on purpose, because AlSi10Mg, the
26: benchmark, breaks it. Each candidate has at most ``--k-max`` additions (sparse sub-systems)
27: and at least ``--min-total`` wt% of additions in all (default 3; 6063 has about 1, the
28: Scalmalloy-type benchmark about 6, AlSi10Mg about 10).
29: 
30: Existing points come from ``seeds.csv`` (baselines, dosing checks, agent picks; use measured
31: compositions once there are any). The default element set is what is on hand or shipping per
32: #146 on 2026-11-13: Mn, Cr, Mg, Ti, Er and Zn from ESPI, plus Si through 4047 powder. Sn (cap
33: 0.1 wt%) and Sc (the mineral the campaign is trying to avoid; D2 already covers it) are left
34: out. Add Zr with ``--elements ... Zr`` once it is on the shelf.
35: 
36: After the CALPHAD screen, pick in descriptor space instead of composition space, since that
37: is what the downstream nodes take as input:
38: 
39:     python bofn-seeding/seed_design.py --candidates screen.csv --features freezing_range csc
40: 
41: ``screen.csv`` needs the feature columns, and an ``existing`` column set to 1 on the rows
42: that are already chosen (benchmarks, agent picks).

Skill directory: /workspace/.skills/citation-integrity

- Always cite sources for claims, either to a primary source or a subagent task.
- Every primary source needs a full BibTeX entry. Cite from the BibTeX, not from a narrative answer.
- Never cite yourself or guess citations from memory.

## Web sources

Every source you use from the `e14c.web` tools needs a full BibTeX entry.

- When you write an entry yourself, name its key with the first author's surname, the year, and the first word of the title, for example `jumper2021highly`. This keeps keys unique.
- Save each entry with `e14c.web.save_citation(bibtex)` as soon as you use the source. It appends the entry to your own file in the project's citations folder, `$WORKSPACE_PATH/citations/$PROJECT_ID/$TRAJECTORY_ID.bib`. In a chat session, `TRAJECTORY_ID` is the session ID. Do not write citation files any other way.

### Sources with a DOI

Call `await e14c.web.cite_doi(doi)`. It fetches the BibTeX from doi.org and saves it. This works for Crossref and DataCite DOIs, including arXiv DOIs such as `10.48550/arXiv.1706.03762`. Check that the title and authors in the returned entry match the paper you read.

### Sources without a DOI

Write the BibTeX entry yourself. Take every field from the source, never from memory.

- Use `@online` for web pages, database records, datasets, software, and reports. The report template hides URLs for most entry types, but it always prints them for `@online`, so readers can find the source.
- Include `author`, `title`, `url`, and `urldate`. `urldate` is the date you accessed the page, written as `YYYY-MM-DD`. Add `date` when the page shows a publication or update date.
- When there is no personal author, put the organization in `author` inside double braces, such as `{{UniProt Consortium}}`. The double braces stop it from being split into first and last names. Use the organization's short name in the key.
- When the page has no date, use the access year in the key.
- Many scholarly pages list their title, authors, and date in `citation_*` meta tags. `(await e14c.web.fetch_page(url)).text` returns the raw HTML so you can read them.
- In `title`, escape `&`, `%`, `_`, and `#` with a backslash, and wrap acronyms in braces to keep their capitals. Do not escape anything in `url`.
- For a journal article with no DOI, use `@article` with `journal`, `volume`, `number`, `pages`, and `year` instead. These fields let a reader find it without a link.

```bibtex
@online{uniprot2026uniprotkb,
  author  = {{UniProt Consortium}},
  title   = {{UniProtKB} entry {P04637} ({P53\_HUMAN}): Cellular tumor antigen p53},
  url     = {https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P04637/entry},
  urldate = {2026-10-12},
}
```

def optimize_acqf_discrete(
    acq_function: AcquisitionFunction,
    q: int,
    choices: Tensor,
    max_batch_size: int = 2048,
    unique: bool = True,
    return_acq_values: bool = True,
    X_avoid: Tensor | None = None,
    inequality_constraints: list[tuple[Tensor, Tensor, float]] | None = None,
) -> tuple[Tensor, Tensor]:
    r"""Optimize over a discrete set of points using batch evaluation.

    For ``q > 1`` this function generates candidates by means of sequential
    conditioning (rather than joint optimization), since for all but the
    smalles number of choices the set ``choices^q`` of discrete points to
    evaluate quickly explodes.

    Args:
        acq_function: An AcquisitionFunction.
        q: The number of candidates.
        choices: A ``num_choices x d`` tensor of possible choices.
        max_batch_size: The maximum number of choices to evaluate in batch.
            A large limit can cause excessive memory usage if the model has
            a large training set.
        unique: If True return unique choices, o/w choices may be repeated
            (only relevant if ``q > 1``).
        X_avoid: An ``n x d`` tensor of candidates that we aren't allowed to pick.
            These will be removed from the set of choices.
        inequality constraints: A list of tuples (indices, coefficients, rhs),
            with each tuple encoding an inequality constraint of the form
            ``\sum_i (X[indices[i]] * coefficients[i]) >= rhs``.
            Infeasible points will be removed from the set of choices.
        return_acq_values: Return acquisition values.
            Can be set to False to avoid memory
            intensive joint forward evaluation of the acquisition function.

    Returns:
        A two-element tuple containing

        - a ``q x d``-dim tensor of generated candidates.
        - an associated acquisition value.
    """
    if isinstance(acq_function, OneShotAcquisitionFunction):
        raise UnsupportedError(
            "Discrete optimization is not supported for one-shot acquisition functions."
        )
    if X_avoid is not None and unique:
        choices = _filter_invalid(X=choices, X_avoid=X_avoid)
    if inequality_constraints is not None:
        choices = _filter_infeasible(
            X=choices, inequality_constraints=inequality_constraints
        )
    len_choices = len(choices)
    if len_choices == 0:
        message = "`choices` must be non-empty."
        if X_avoid is not None or inequality_constraints is not None:
            message += (
                " No feasible points remain after removing `X_avoid` and "
                "filtering out infeasible points."
            )
        raise InputDataError(message)
    elif len_choices < q and unique:
        warnings.warn(
            (
                f"Requested {q=} candidates from fully discrete search "
                f"space, but only {len_choices} possible choices remain. "
            ),
            OptimizationWarning,
            stacklevel=2,
        )
        q = len_choices
    choices_batched = choices.unsqueeze(-2)
    if q > 1:
        candidate_list, acq_value_list = [], []
        base_X_pending = acq_function.X_pending
        for _ in range(q):
            with torch.no_grad():
                acq_values = _split_batch_eval_acqf(
                    acq_function=acq_function,
                    X=choices_batched,
                    max_batch_size=max_batch_size,
                )
            best_idx = torch.argmax(acq_values)
            candidate_list.append(choices_batched[best_idx])
            acq_value_list.append(acq_values[best_idx])
            # set pending points
            candidates = torch.cat(candidate_list, dim=-2)
            acq_function.set_X_pending(
                torch.cat([base_X_pending, candidates], dim=-2)
                if base_X_pending is not None
                else candidates
            )
            # need to remove choice from choice set if enforcing uniqueness
            if unique:
                choices_batched = torch.cat(
                    [choices_batched[:best_idx], choices_batched[best_idx + 1 :]]
                )

        # Reset acq_func to previous X_pending state
        acq_function.set_X_pending(base_X_pending)
        best_acq_values = torch.stack(acq_value_list)

    else:
        with torch.no_grad():
            acq_values = _split_batch_eval_acqf(
                acq_function=acq_function,
                X=choices_batched,
                max_batch_size=max_batch_size,
            )
        best_idx = torch.argmax(acq_values)
        candidates = choices_batched[best_idx]
        best_acq_values = acq_values[best_idx]

    if not return_acq_values:
        return candidates, None
    return candidates, best_acq_values

## Abstract

The expansion of the material library for the laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process is essential for the further establishment of the process in areas such as the aerospace and automotive industries. In this study, we designed a high-strength and low-cost Al-Mn-Ti-Zr alloy specifically tailored to the unique conditions of the LPBF process. Gas-atomized pre-alloyed powder was prepared and used as feedstock to fabricate LPBF specimens for microstructural examination and mechanical testing. By taking advantage of the high solidification rate, unconventionally large amounts of Mn (3.7 ± 0.5 wt%) are metastably frozen within the α-Al matrix, contributing significantly to solid solution hardening (~104 MPa ≙ 37% share of yield strength). The as-built specimens exhibit a yield strength of 284 ± 3 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength of 320 ± 1 MPa, and an elongation at fracture of 16.9 ± 0.2%. This new alloy exhibits a bimodal microstructure consisting of alternately distributed fine equiaxed and coarse columnar grain regions. Further microstructural analyses reveal a high number of primary L12 cubic Al3(Tix Zr1 - x) nanoparticles within the equiaxed α-Al grains near the bottom of the melt pool. A highly coherent interface with the α-Al matrix confirms high efficiency for heterogeneous nucleation during solidification. In addition to the Al3(Tix Zr1 - x) nanoparticles, an AlxMn(Fe, Si) phase with a quasi-crystalline structure is observed along the grain boundaries and interdendritic areas.

## 1. Introduction

Sequential Model-Based Optimization (SMBO) algorithms are techniques for the optimization of problems for which the evaluation of solution candidates is resource-intensive, such as problems requiring real physical experiments or problems that require computationally-expensive simulations. The latter are particularly present in almost any application of Artificial Intelligence, most notably in terms of parameter tuning problems – a problem that is also omnipresent in Evolutionary Computation (Lobo et al., 2007). SMBO-based techniques are among the most successfully applied hyper-parameter tuning methods (Hutter et al., 2011; Bartz-Beielstein, 2010; Falkner et al., 2018; Kotthoff et al., 2019), so that research on this family of iterative optimization heuristics has gained significant traction in the last decade. SMBO forms today an integral part of the state-of-the-art heuristic solvers. Its probably best-known representatives are Bayesian Optimization (see surveys by (Shahriari et al., 2016; Mockus, 1989; Rasmussen and Williams, 2006)) and, in particular, Efficient Global Optimization (EGO, (Jones et al., 1998)).

The generic SMBO method works as follows. An initial design of points is sampled and evaluated with the true objective function. The eponymous sequential part iteratively (1) builds a surrogate of the true objective function (on basis of the already evaluated samples), (2) proposes new samples by optimizing a so-called infill-criterion (which is sometimes referred to as acquisition function), (3) evaluates these additional samples, and (4) integrates these samples, together with their quality indicators (“function values”, “fitness”) into the memory. Each of these steps offers a great variety of design choices, which all may affect the performance of the SMBO procedure. Which surrogate model should be used? Which of the countless infill criteria to use? What method should be used to create the initial sample and what proportion of the overall budget should be spent on the initial design? While a large body of works addresses the first two questions (see surveys mentioned above), the latter two questions are treated rather poorly. In this work we aim to shed light on the relevance of a suitably chosen initial sampling strategy. More precisely, we study how the size of the initial design and the strategy used to generate it affects the performance of SMBO. As a well-established benchmark environment offering a great variety of different numerical optimization problems, we chose the 24 noiseless BBOB functions (in different dimensions) as test-bed for our investigation.

Our setup comprises of varying the initial design strategy (classical uniform and Latin-Hypercube-Sampling (LHS) as the most frequently used methods and quasi-random Halton and Sobol’ sequences), the total budget, and the fraction of this total budget that is used to build the initial sample. ## Abstract

Conventional precipitation-hardened aluminum alloys experience severe mechanical degradation above 200 °C due to precipitate coarsening and dissolution. This study presents a novel Al–Fe-Mg Zr eutectic alloy fabricated via laser powder bed fusion, achieving crack-free fabrication with 99.8% relative density, ultrafine grains, and a heterogeneous cellular-lamellar microstructure. Direct aging (400 °C/4 h) enhances yield strength (YS) to 376.1 MPa (72.6% increase) and ultimate tensile strength to 405.8 MPa (30.7% increase) compared to the as-printed condition, while reducing ductility to 11.1%. The strengthening mechanisms arise from grain boundary strengthening, precipitation strengthening via coherent L12-Al3Zr nanoscale dispersoids, dislocation strengthening, and effective load transfer through submicron-scale Al–Fe intermetallic phases. High-temperature tensile testing reveals excellent mechanical stability, retaining a YS of 124 MPa at 350 °C. After prolonged thermal exposure (400 °C/100 h), the alloy maintains good mechanical properties, demonstrating excellent heat resistance due to the low coarsening rate of Al13Fe4 (0.98 nm 3/s) and sustained Al3Zr precipitates. The dual-scale strengthening strategy significantly advances developing high-strength and thermally stable Al alloys for high performance applications.

This study presents a novel Al–Fe-Mg Zr eutectic alloy fabricated via laser powder bed fusion, achieving crack-free fabrication with 99.8% relative density, ultrafine grains, and a heterogeneous cellular-lamellar microstructure. Direct aging (400 °C/4 h) enhances yield strength (YS) to 376.1 MPa (72.6% increase) and ultimate tensile strength to 405.8 MPa (30.7% increase) compared to the as-printed condition, while reducing ductility to 11.1%. The strengthening mechanisms arise from grain boundary strengthening, precipitation strengthening via coherent L12-Al3Zr nanoscale dispersoids, dislocation strengthening, and effective load transfer through submicron-scale Al–Fe intermetallic phases. High-temperature tensile testing reveals excellent mechanical stability, retaining a YS of 124 MPa at 350 °C. After prolonged thermal exposure (400 °C/100 h), the alloy maintains good mechanical properties, demonstrating excellent heat resistance due to the low coarsening rate of Al13Fe4 (0.98 nm 3/s) and sustained Al3Zr precipitates. The dual-scale strengthening strategy significantly advances developing high-strength and thermally stable Al alloys for high performance applications.
