## Abstract

Sequential model-based optimization (SMBO) approaches are algorithms for solving problems that require computationally or otherwise expensive function evaluations. The key design principle of SMBO is a substitution of the true objective function by a surrogate, which is used to propose the point(s) to be evaluated next.

SMBO algorithms are intrinsically modular, leaving the user with many important design choices. Significant research efforts go into understanding which settings perform best for which type of problems. Most works, however, focus on the choice of the model, the acquisition function, and the strategy used to optimize the latter. The choice of the initial sampling strategy, however, receives much less attention. Not surprisingly, quite diverging recommendations can be found in the literature.

We analyze in this work how the size and the distribution of the initial sample influences the overall quality of the efficient global optimization (EGO) algorithm, a well-known SMBO approach. While, overall, small initial budgets using Halton sampling seem preferable, we also observe that the performance landscape is rather unstructured. We furthermore identify several situations in which EGO performs unfavorably against random sampling. Both observations indicate that an adaptive SMBO design could be beneficial, making SMBO an interesting test-bed for automated algorithm design.

## Abstract

Al-Ce alloys are known to retain a large fraction of their room temperature properties at elevated temperatures and after exposure to temperature for extended periods. Here we work with the ternary close-to-eutectic alloy Al-10Ce-4Mg and explore the effect of extrusion on its microstructure and mechanical properties. Extrusion produces a highly refined microstructure with texture exhibiting a twofold increase in strength (tensile strength of 390 MPa at room temperature) and fourfold increase in failure strain relative to the as cast state. After exposure to 300 °C for 100 h the alloy retains 82% and 88% of the room temperature strength in the as-cast and extruded states, respectively. The ratio of the strength at 300 °C to the strength at room temperature is 0.4, below the corresponding ratio for the Al-10Ce binary alloy (ratio 0.7) but higher than that of AA2618 (ratio 0.1). The extruded Al-10Ce-4Mg has fracture toughness of 23 kJ/m 2, which is retained in proportion of 97.6% after exposure to 300 °C for 100 h. The material exhibits negative strain rate sensitivity at room temperature and in the range of strain rates \(\:{10}^{-5}\:{s}^{-1}\) to \(\:{10}^{-2}\:{s}^{-1}\). We show that the high room temperature strength is due to Al 11 Ce 3 dispersoids and Mg-rich precipitates. The Mg-rich precipitates dissolve in the temperature range 200 °C to 250 °C while the Al 11 Ce 3 dispersoids remain stable and provide strengthening at 300 °C. Mg-rich precipitates reform upon cooling, which ensures property retention upon thermal cycling. The high toughness, strength and property retention upon exposure to elevated temperatures make this alloy an excellent candidate for applications requiring lightweight temperature resistant materials.

## Introduction

A need exists for light materials with enhanced thermal stability to be used in supersonic aircraft design. The use of Al alloys would provide higher fuel savings, lower CO 2 emissions, and overall increased energy efficiency. However, the use of current Al alloys from the AA2XXX and AA7XXX class, which are precipitate hardened, is impossible as their properties degrade above ~ 200\(\:℃\) due to the dissolution and/or coarsening of precipitates(Gao et al. 2019)(Mondol et al. 2017). In contrast, the Al-Ce intermetallics are highly stable and resist coarsening up to at least 350 °C (Guo et al. 2022, Shen et al. 2023, Nam et al. 2023, Singh et al. 2024). This drives the emergence of a new generation of castable Al-Ce alloys with significantly improved high-temperature strength (Shen et al. 2023, Stojanovic et al. 2018, Sims et al. 2016, El-Hadad et al. 2023, Weiss and Cerium 2019, Huda and Edi 2013).

Ce is a relatively abundant rare earth element (REE) which may be obtained as a byproduct of the extraction and purification of more valuable REEs, including Li, Pr, Nd, Dy, and Tb (Sims et al. 2022). Cerium lacks high-volume applications at present time (Weiss and Cerium 2019, Czerwinski 2019). When added to Al as an alloying element, Ce forms the Al 11 Ce 3 intermetallic, with an eutectic point at 10% Ce (Sims et al. 2017) (all percentages in wt%). Microstructures with off-eutectic compositions contain a dominant Al (fcc) phase for hypoeutectic, and script-like (or plate-shaped) Al 11 Ce 3 intermetallics in the case of hypereutectic alloys (Perrin et al. 2023, Okamoto 2011, Cao et al. 2017, Dai et al. 2023, Sun et al. 2019, Kozakevich et al. 2023, Ye et al. 2023, Rogachev and Naumova 2021). The non-uniform distribution of the intermetallics in the as-cast state leads to sub-optimal strengthening. Nevertheless, Al-Ce alloys in the near-eutectic range (5–15% Ce) exhibit excellent castability and resistance to hot tearing and cracking (Plotkowski et al. 2020).

# Effect of precipitation-forming elements in a near-eutectic Al-Ce alloy for Laser Powder Bed Fusion

Additive manufacturing. Published: 2022-06-10. 23 citations.

## Abstract

Despite a growing interest in additive manufacturing technologies, there is still a limited selection of suitable materials developed regarding the unique non-equilibrium cooling conditions. A highly promising alloy system for Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) is Al-Ce, which shows outstanding processability in recent studies. The medium strengths already achievable with the binary system are to be improved in these investigations by additional precipitation-forming elements. By adding Mg and Si, a very high tensile strength of 593 MPa in the as-built condition can be achieved. XRD measurements show that the addition of these two elements lead to additional formation of an AlCeSi phase and phases of the Mg2Si precipitation sequence, which affects the usually expected eutectic formation of the Al11Ce3 phase. Contrary to the expected dominance of the binary intermetallics, AlCeSi in particular can be identified. The Al11Ce3 content in the microstructure can only be significantly increased with modified parameter combinations or volume energy inputs. Along with this, additional differences in grain size and grain morphology can be identified by EBSD investigations. The influence of the parameters extend to different mechanical properties as a function of the applied parameter combinations. With the very good additive processability in the form of wide process parameter windows, the parameter combinations can be used to adjust the properties in the as-built state.

## 7\. Conclusions

In this paper we have presented a database for data-driven investigations of the sequential model-based optimization (SMBO) strategy EGO *([Jones et al., 1998](https://arxiv.org/html/2003.13826#bib.bib31))*. The focus of our work is on analyzing the influence of the (size and type of) initial design on the overall performance of EGO. Our data base contains data for 720 different problems, which are evaluated against a total of 40 different initial design strategies.

While we clearly observed that small initial designs are preferable at a high-level view, we also found that each of the 40 considered combinations of design type and size achieved best performance on at least one of the 720 problems. Our findings thus confirm that an automated strategy selection method – like the proof-of-concept approach presented in *([Saini et al., 2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2003.13826#bib.bib48))* – might indeed be profitable. Moreover, we even identified cases in which the usage of EGO does not provide any benefits over the initial (quasi-)random sample – especially in case of highly multimodal problems.

Our long-term vision are SMBO approaches that dynamically decide whether to take the next sample from a (quasi-)random distribution or whether to derive it from the surrogate model. Going one step further, we believe that an adaptive choice of the acquisition function, and possibly even of the solver used to optimize the latter, should bring substantial performance gains – in particular in the case in which the total budget is known in advance. Hence, we need to “train” a final recommendation (last evaluation) instead of achieving good anytime performance. These two mentioned questions fall under the umbrella of dynamic algorithm configuration, which has been an important driver for the field of evolutionary computation for the last decades *([Burke et al., 2013](https://arxiv.org/html/2003.13826#bib.bib13); [Eiben et al., 1999](https://arxiv.org/html/2003.13826#bib.bib18); [Karafotias et al., 2015](https://arxiv.org/html/2003.13826#bib.bib32); [Doerr and Doerr, 2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2003.13826#bib.bib17))*, and which has recently also gained interest in machine learning communities *([Biedenkapp et al., 2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2003.13826#bib.bib6))*.

Typically, the budget of common SMBO applications is too small for a classical a priori (i.e., offline) landscape-aware selection of the optimizer design based on supervised learning approaches (see *([Kerschke et al., 2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2003.13826#bib.bib33))* for a survey). However, in case high-level properties – such as the degree of (multi-)modality or the sizes of the problem’s attraction basins – are known for the problem at hand, or can be guessed by an expert, selecting a suitable initial design strategy is feasible.

Finally, we have seen that the performance of the different designs was often quite comparable. To investigate the differences in more detail, we suggest to consider the different strategies as a portfolio of different algorithms. With this viewpoint, one could analyze the marginal contributions *([Xu et al., 2012](https://arxiv.org/html/2003.13826#bib.bib52))* or Shapley values *([Fréchette et al., 2016](https://arxiv.org/html/2003.13826#bib.bib21))* of the different designs, and leverage the information contained therein.

{"code": "answer = r'''## Bottom line

I would retain the mixed seed strategy and a **provisional 6–7-seed target**, but the draft does not yet justify either that exact count or a general IMSE-over-maximin recommendation. Its strongest point is the warning about delayed strength feedback.

## 1. Corrections to the draft

- **“[Bossek et al.] found that an initial design of about 30 % of the budget did best on their benchmark suite.”** Replace with: “They generally favored small initial designs, with substantial problem dependence.” Their [conclusion](https://doi.org/10.1145/3377930.3390155) does not establish a general 30% optimum.
- **“Keep the three-way mix, but use about 6–7 seeds rather than 9.”** The proposed schedule still has **eight pre-optimizer runs**: D1, D2, B30, B15, S1–S4. Including D1-r and four finalist runs leaves exactly 12 optimizer runs. Identify which slot is removed/merged; relabeling dosing checks does not release budget. The toy instead gives *all* nonseed runs to optimization, without these reservations.
- **“Maximin sends every point to a corner.”** Change to “Maximin selected boundary-heavy points in this pool and metric.” Likewise, “hardest ... to melt, dose and print” is an untested feasibility judgment, not an output of the comparison.
- **“Each element one alloy has and the other doesn't adds 0.5 to the distance.”** It adds **0.25 to squared distance**. This distinction materially affects interpreting the exclusion radius.
- **“Exclusion starts to matter once the existing set is large: literature points, or a dense CALPHAD screen.”** A screen is a *candidate pool*, not observed coverage. Only genuinely available observations, with appropriate noise/fidelity, should count as existing information.

## 2. Code audit and executed checks

I reproduced `space_filling_compare.csv` to its reported precision and completed the full **30-replicate × two-scenario × eight-policy** budget rerun.

| Method | Mean nearest distance ↓ | Fill distance ↓ | Mean posterior variance ↓ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Sobol | 1.0290 | 1.8104 | 0.9277 |
| Maximin | 1.1056 | **1.7153** | 0.9548 |
| IMSE | **0.9550** | 1.7595 | **0.8950** |

**`seed_design.py`:**

- **Scaling is a modeling assumption.** Dividing by caps equates the full Ti range (0.5 wt%) with the full Si range (12 wt%). That is not automatically the campaign GP’s geometry: it assumes fixed bounds, equal length scales, and the additional presence features. Descriptor mode uses dataset-wide min–max scaling; freeze those bounds, handle correlated descriptors, and retain composition information where descriptors are insufficient.
- **The element-set term double-counts identity** relative to composition coordinates and jumps at *any* positive concentration. Trace impurities in measured compositions could switch every element “on.” Use a declared intentional-addition/detection threshold and test weights including zero. With weight 0.5, any different support already has distance ≥0.5: the default exclusion radius mostly tests same-support alloys. Seed-0’s pool actually contains **130 candidates** within radius 0.5 of existing points; exclusion is not intrinsically inactive, just inactive for the first selections.
- **The ≥3 wt% filter is unjustified as a strength screen.** It excludes lean precipitation-strengthened candidates—the goal includes reducing mineral burden. Remove it or demonstrate sensitivity. The reference measure also favors three-addition faces: 7,172 of 11,136 default candidates have three additions. “Average coverage” means coverage under this chosen face-sampling distribution, not uniform coverage of all plausible alloys.
- **IMSE algebra checks out** against direct posterior-variance reduction. But it assumes a noiseless, unit-amplitude radial-basis-function GP with fixed isotropic length scale 0.5. Treating *planned* seeds as noiseless observations is optimistic if they fail or remain unmeasured. Include observation noise and node-specific availability. My three-scramble checks retained IMSE’s average-coverage advantage at length scales 0.25, 0.5 and 1, and after removing the set penalty or total-addition cutoff; that is useful sensitivity evidence, not strength-performance validation.
- Rerun with **two** space-filling additions, changed B15, and actual S1/S2: the reported comparison uses three additions around the old five-row `seeds.csv`.

**`budget_split_sim.py`:**

- NumPy problems are paired, but **PyTorch acquisition sampling/fitting is not seeded**. My rerun gave 2+3+1 minus 3+3+3 = **+0.0479 ± 0.0164**, using one standard error across 30 problem clusters. Direction reproduced; exact supplied values did not. The two scenarios reuse the same 30 problems, so they are **not 60 independent instances**; cluster by problem when combining them.
- Baselines all cluster around **one** known bump—not distinct AlSi10Mg and Scalmalloy families. “Agent right” knows the optimum center and active dimensions; “wrong” merely revisits a good family, rather than proposing poor/unprintable alloys. This favors the claim that mistaken agents cost little.
- “Beat baseline” uses the best of **two versus three** baseline points, changing the threshold between policies. Use one fixed reference. “All 25 Sobol” is actually **two baselines + 23 Sobol**; rename it or implement the label.
- `unique=True` prevents duplication **within a batch only**. The pool is never depleted and previous observations are not excluded; my diagnostic found one cross-batch repeat. Explicitly permit/budget replication or exclude observed points. Log rather than suppress GP-fitting failures.
- Discrete-pool qLogEI is a reasonable **controlled flat-BO toy**, not a BOFN/p-KGFN surrogate. Seeds can lie off-pool; the optimizer cannot. Check larger pools or continuous optimization, noisy expected improvement, and especially delayed/partial feedback, feasibility and reserved confirmation runs. No seven-seed policy, IMSE seed policy, or maximin seed policy is tested here.

## 3. Is the disagreement resolved?

**Only conditionally.** IMSE wins the average-error criterion it targets; maximin wins the reported worst-case fill distance. Neither demonstrates better optimization. Boundary attraction is expected when maximizing separation, not an implementation bug.

I would prefer maximin when kernel length scales or reference-density weights are unreliable, when rare alloy families and worst-case coverage matter, or after a credible manufacturability screen removes unsafe extremes. A useful compromise is IMSE with a minimum-distance constraint, selected over a **physically reachable** pool. Do not let an equilibrium-only CALPHAD cutoff discard the supersaturated/metastable mechanisms being sought.

## 4. Proposed alloys and feedstock

**D1/D2 are sensible process-matched controls.** Commercial powder and wrought 6063 are valuable but cannot replace controls through the campaign’s own atomization/printing route. Keep B30 and an element-specific B15 only if they resolve separate, consequential dosing uncertainties.

**S1 is a defensible mechanism probe, not a demonstrated winner:** its [reported 284 MPa yield strength](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jallcom.2021.163156) overlaps the draft’s AlSi10Mg range and is below aged Scalmalloy. Its nucleation strategy also overlaps D2; Mn supersaturation is the important distinction.

**S2 needs a substantive correction.** The quoted **376 MPa yield strength** comes from [Li et al.](https://doi.org/10.1080/17452759.2025.2516663), whose measured printed alloy is **Al–1.87Fe–1.02Mg–1.03Zr**, not Al–(3–5)Fe–1Mg–(0.5–0.7)Zr. Those are different hypotheses. Use the documented chemistry or explicitly withdraw the property attribution. Al–10Ce is not automatically a better fallback: it violates the Ce cap, carries 10 wt% listed critical additions, and lacks a compelling room-temperature strength advantage as presented.

The Zr/Fe/Ce procurement warning is sound, but a purchase order is insufficient: establish delivery, carrier composition, dissolution time/temperature, recovery, and contamination. **Mass-balance the 6063 cups and master-alloy carriers**; nominally pure-Al candidates may be unreachable. Verify bulk chemistry, powder size/yield and oxygen before claiming literature transfer.

## 5. Prioritized changes before Dec 18

1. **Freeze success criteria:** yield versus ultimate strength, matched heat treatment/orientation, minimum ductility/density, and uncertainty-aware superiority. Define a dated mineral metric explicitly excluding/including Al; Sc-free is not synonymous with low burden.
2. **Fix the 25-run ledger and S2 attribution**, then commit to purchasable, reachable recipes. Consider a low-Sc bridge seed if matching aged Scalmalloy is central; zero-Sc and D2 alone weakly resolve that trade-off.
3. **Write a node-by-date data-availability contract.** Seed tensile results arrive Jan 19–22, not when bars print. Advance a sentinel tensile test if possible; otherwise label the first two batches as prior-driven for strength, while incorporating measured upstream evidence and pending evaluations.
4. **Freeze the executable optimization protocol:** objective, constraints, source-specific noise/fidelity, failures, pending points, repeats, and common seeds/budgets for policy comparisons. Dry-run the entire ingestion-to-batch pipeline.
5. **Rerun seed selection on the final screened pool**, with actual seeds, two additions, declared scaling/reference weights, and sensitivity checks—not the present default demonstration.

**Review choices:** I treated the attachments as the schedule authority; I clustered uncertainty by independent synthetic problem; I separated average prediction coverage from optimization performance and matched-condition strength claims.

[Executed checks, rerun tables, code and saved references](review_checks/review_evidence.zip).
'''

## Bottom line

I would retain the mixed seed strategy and a **provisional 6–7-seed target**, but the draft does not yet justify either that exact count or a general IMSE-over-maximin recommendation. Its strongest point is the warning about delayed strength feedback.

## 1. Corrections to the draft

- **“[Bossek et al.] found that an initial design of about 30 % of the budget did best on their benchmark suite.”** Replace with: “They generally favored small initial designs, with substantial problem dependence.” Their [conclusion](https://doi.org/10.1145/3377930.3390155) does not establish a general 30% optimum.
- **“Keep the three-way mix, but use about 6–7 seeds rather than 9.”** The proposed schedule still has **eight pre-optimizer runs**: D1, D2, B30, B15, S1–S4. Including D1-r and four finalist runs leaves exactly 12 optimizer runs. Identify which slot is removed/merged; relabeling dosing checks does not release budget. The toy instead gives *all* nonseed runs to optimization, without these reservations.
- **“Maximin sends every point to a corner.”** Change to “Maximin selected boundary-heavy points in this pool and metric.” Likewise, “hardest ... to melt, dose and print” is an untested feasibility judgment, not an output of the comparison.
- **“Each element one alloy has and the other doesn't adds 0.5 to the distance.”** It adds **0.25 to squared distance**. This distinction materially affects interpreting the exclusion radius.
- **“Exclusion starts to matter once the existing set is large: literature points, or a dense CALPHAD screen.”** A screen is a *candidate pool*, not observed coverage. Only genuinely available observations, with appropriate noise/fidelity, should count as existing information.

## 2. Code audit and executed checks

I reproduced `space_filling_compare.csv` to its reported precision and completed the full **30-replicate × two-scenario × eight-policy** budget rerun.

| Method | Mean nearest distance ↓ | Fill distance ↓ | Mean posterior variance ↓ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Sobol | 1.0290 | 1.8104 | 0.9277 |
| Maximin | 1.1056 | **1.7153** | 0.9548 |
| IMSE | **0.9550** | 1.7595 | **0.8950** |

**`seed_design.py`:**

- **Scaling is a modeling assumption.** Dividing by caps equates the full Ti range (0.5 wt%) with the full Si range (12 wt%). That is not automatically the campaign GP’s geometry: it assumes fixed bounds, equal length scales, and the additional presence features. Descriptor mode uses dataset-wide min–max scaling; freeze those bounds, handle correlated descriptors, and retain composition information where descriptors are insufficient.
- **The element-set term double-counts identity** relative to composition coordinates and jumps at *any* positive concentration. Trace impurities in measured compositions could switch every element “on.” Use a declared intentional-addition/detection threshold and test weights including zero. With weight 0.5, any different support already has distance ≥0.5: the default exclusion radius mostly tests same-support alloys. Seed-0’s pool actually contains **130 candidates** within radius 0.5 of existing points; exclusion is not intrinsically inactive, just inactive for the first selections.
- **The ≥3 wt% filter is unjustified as a strength screen.** It excludes lean precipitation-strengthened candidates—the goal includes reducing mineral burden. Remove it or demonstrate sensitivity. The reference measure also favors three-addition faces: 7,172 of 11,136 default candidates have three additions. “Average coverage” means coverage under this chosen face-sampling distribution, not uniform coverage of all plausible alloys.
- **IMSE algebra checks out** against direct posterior-variance reduction. But it assumes a noiseless, unit-amplitude radial-basis-function GP with fixed isotropic length scale 0.5. Treating *planned* seeds as noiseless observations is optimistic if they fail or remain unmeasured. Include observation noise and node-specific availability. My three-scramble checks retained IMSE’s average-coverage advantage at length scales 0.25, 0.5 and 1, and after removing the set penalty or total-addition cutoff; that is useful sensitivity evidence, not strength-performance validation.
- Rerun with **two** space-filling additions, changed B15, and actual S1/S2: the reported comparison uses three additions around the old five-row `seeds.csv`.

**`budget_split_sim.py`:**

- NumPy problems are paired, but **PyTorch acquisition sampling/fitting is not seeded**. My rerun gave 2+3+1 minus 3+3+3 = **+0.0479 ± 0.0164**, using one standard error across 30 problem clusters. Direction reproduced; exact supplied values did not. The two scenarios reuse the same 30 problems, so they are **not 60 independent instances**; cluster by problem when combining them.
- Baselines all cluster around **one** known bump—not distinct AlSi10Mg and Scalmalloy families. “Agent right” knows the optimum center and active dimensions; “wrong” merely revisits a good family, rather than proposing poor/unprintable alloys. This favors the claim that mistaken agents cost little.
- “Beat baseline” uses the best of **two versus three** baseline points, changing the threshold between policies. Use one fixed reference. “All 25 Sobol” is actually **two baselines + 23 Sobol**; rename it or implement the label.
- `unique=True` prevents duplication **within a batch only**. The pool is never depleted and previous observations are not excluded; my diagnostic found one cross-batch repeat. Explicitly permit/budget replication or exclude observed points. Log rather than suppress GP-fitting failures.
- Discrete-pool qLogEI is a reasonable **controlled flat-BO toy**, not a BOFN/p-KGFN surrogate. Seeds can lie off-pool; the optimizer cannot. Check larger pools or continuous optimization, noisy expected improvement, and especially delayed/partial feedback, feasibility and reserved confirmation runs. No seven-seed policy, IMSE seed policy, or maximin seed policy is tested here.

IMSE needs declared kernel hyperparameters, not a fitted GP. Boundary attraction is expected when maximizing separation, not an implementation bug.

============================== README.md ==============================

# Seeding the BOFN campaign: which experiments come first (#275)

[#275](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/275) asks how to choose the
initial experiments for the Al alloy campaign in
[#255](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/255), which
[#256](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/256) schedules. It suggests
a mix of three sources, about three runs each:

- **agent-chosen** compositions (literature, databases, CALPHAD);
- **known baselines** (AlSi10Mg, Scalmalloy);
- **Sobol** or another space-filling design.

It also asks:

- how to bring in the databases from [#7](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/7)
  and [#8](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/8);
- how "fantasy" data (synthetic, or from the literature) could stand in until real data exist;
- whether 3 + 3 + 3 makes sense with 25 experiments left.

Edison Scientific was the rubber duck: two `LITERATURE_HIGH` reviews and a critique of this
draft. They're in [`edison/`](edison/).

**Status:** this is a plan. Nothing here has been run on a real sample. The compositions are
proposals. They still need the CALPHAD screen, the design-space freeze, and a check of what is
actually on the shelf.

## Short answers

**On 3 + 3 + 3 with 25 left:** keep the three-way mix, but use about 6–7 seeds rather than 9. Give
the runs this frees up to the optimizer.

- **Edison's verdict on 9 seeds is "slightly too many".** Nine seeds are 36 % of the 25 runs.
  Bossek et al. (2020, [10.1145/3377930.3390155](https://doi.org/10.1145/3377930.3390155)) found
  that an initial design of about 30 % of the budget did best on their benchmark suite. Edison
  suggests 3 baselines, 2 agent picks, 2 space-filling points, 14 optimizer runs and 4 finalist
  runs ([q1](edison/q1-seeding-strategy/artifact-00.md)).
- **A toy simulation agrees on the direction** ([below](#how-many-seeds-a-toy-check)). Across 60
  paired problem instances, 2 baselines + 3 agent + 1 space-filling beat 3 + 3 + 3 by
  0.043 ± 0.014 in the best value found. It beat the best baseline 75 % of the time, against
  55 % for 3 + 3 + 3. 3 + 3 + 3 did worst of all the optimizer splits when the agent picks only
  pointed back at the known alloy family. That is the circularity risk Edison also flags.
- **Don't add a third baseline run.** The 6063 runs (A1–A5) and commercial AlSi10Mg powder at P1
  are baselines that cost no design run. D1-r stays: it measures the benchmark's own spread
  ([#256](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/blob/claude/issue-256-20261112-2149/al-campaign-schedule/README.md#the-36-al-runs)).

**In the schedule's terms** ([table](#a-proposed-seed-set)):

- D1 and D2 are the baselines.
- S1–S2 are agent picks, with different strengthening mechanisms.
- S3–S4 are space-filling picks from [`seed_design.py`](seed_design.py), made after the CALPHAD
  screen trims the candidate pool.
- B30 stays a dosing check. B15 should check the element the agent picks depend on (Mn, or Zr)
  rather than Si a second time.
- If the flex slots X1–X3 (Dec 14–16) aren't needed to redo failed runs, use them as early
  optimizer picks, not as more seeds.

**What matters more than the split:**

1. **The optimizer picks R1 (Dec 18) and R2 (Jan 8) before any new composition has strength
   data.** Seed tensile bars print at P3 (Jan 12–13). Until then, the strength nodes run on
   priors. So the literature data and strength models that go into those priors decide the first
   six optimizer runs ([pseudo-data](#literature-and-fantasy-data)).
2. **Most of the literature's best Sc-free seeds need Zr, Fe, Ce or Cu.** None of these is on
   the Nov 13 list in [#146](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/146#issuecomment-6842840090)
   (Mn, Cr, Zn, Sn, Mg, Sc, Er, Ti from ESPI; Si, Fe, Ni and Cu were never ordered). The
   Scalmalloy-type benchmark D2 needs Zr as well. Check whether Zr is coming. If not, order it as
   an Al–Zr master alloy before the S runs (Dec 7–10).
3. **The design box on [PR #72](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/pull/72)
   excludes several of the best-documented Sc-free LPBF alloys:** Al–10Ce (Ce cap 6 wt%), the
   Al–Fe eutectics (Fe cap 0.5 wt%), and Addalloy-type Al–4.5Mg–1.5Zr (Zr cap 1 wt%). Its
   Mg + Si ≤ 6 wt% joint cap even excludes AlSi10Mg. Settle these at the design-space freeze
   (G0, today).
4. **Settle the mineral-burden metric before picking seeds.** Of the 15 palette elements, only
   Fe, Si and Cu are absent from the USGS 2022 critical minerals list. By a plain wt% count of
   listed elements, Al–4Mn–0.5Ti–0.5Zr (5 wt%) is only a little leaner than Scalmalloy (about
   6 wt%, counting Mg). It wins clearly only if the metric weights Sc's supply risk well above
   Mn's. Fe- and
   Si-based strengthening is where "stronger and leaner" is easiest to show.

**Space-filling:** use the integrated-variance pick (`imse`) around the points already chosen.
Maximin pushes every point into an extreme corner. Sobol with an exclusion radius rarely
excludes anything with this few existing points. In 7-D, three points cover little whatever the
method, so space-fill in a reduced space: CALPHAD descriptors, which are what the downstream
nodes see ([details](#space-filling-around-the-points-we-already-have)).

**"Fantasy" data:** call it pseudo-data, keep it in its own source, and never overwrite it in
place. It isn't BoTorch's `fantasize`
([#104](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/104)).
[Below](#literature-and-fantasy-data).

**The pre-registered AI benchmark:** every policy has to start from the same seed set. If only
the AI policy gets the agent picks, the "acceleration factor" measures a warm start, not the
optimizer. Edison q1, pitfall P9. [Below](#making-the-seeds-count-for-the-paper).

## What the 25 experiments are

The [#256 schedule](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/blob/claude/issue-256-20261112-2149/al-campaign-schedule/README.md#the-36-al-runs)
has 36 Al atomizer runs. Five are the 6063 baseline repeats (A1–A5) and six are flex slots
(X1–X6). That leaves 25 runs whose composition someone has to choose:

| Block | Runs | When | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| D benchmarks | D1 (AlSi10Mg-type), D2 (Scalmalloy-type), D1-r (repeat) | Nov 30, Dec 2, Feb 8 | baseline seeds |
| B dosing checks | B30 (Si ≈ 3.9 wt%), B15 (Si ≈ 2.1 wt%) | Dec 1, Dec 3 | known-composition seeds on the Al–Si line |
| S CALPHAD seeds | S1–S4 | Dec 7–10 | agent-chosen seeds |
| R optimizer rounds | R1–R4, 3 each | Jan 5 – Feb 3 | optimizer |
| F finalists | F1 ×2, F2 ×2 | Jan 25–28 | repeats of optimizer picks |

The schedule already spends 8 runs on seeds before the optimizer's first batch: D1, D2, B30, B15
and S1–S4. D1-r comes late. The flex slots X1–X3 (Dec 14–16) also come before the first batch is
picked on Dec 18. Following Edison (q1, P10), the 6063 repeats and dosing checks count once for
coverage, since each is one composition, but every run counts toward estimating noise.

When strength data arrive matters more than any of this. P2 (Dec 16–17) prints only single tracks
of the S runs. Their cubes and tensile bars come at P3 (Jan 12–13), with tensile tests Jan 19–22.
So when R1 (Dec 18) and R2 (Jan 8) are picked, the only strength data are commercial AlSi10Mg from
P1 and wrought 6063.

## A proposed seed set

| Slot | Strategy | Composition (wt%) | Why | Needs | In the PR #72 box? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1–A5 | baseline (free) | 6063 bar | Run-to-run noise; the dilute end | on hand | yes |
| P1 | baseline (free) | commercial AlSi10Mg powder | Print window, density, tensile and corrosion baselines with no atomizer run | on hand | — |
| D1 | baseline | Al–10Si–0.35Mg | The alloy to beat. As-built YS ≈ 250–350 MPa ([q2](edison/q2-seed-alloys-and-data/artifact-00.md)) | 4047 + Mg | Mg + Si ≤ 6 says no; drop that cap |
| D2 | baseline | Al–4.5Mg–0.7Sc–0.3Zr(–0.5Mn) | The Sc reference. YS 256–278 MPa as-built, 456–469 MPa direct-aged ([10.3390/cryst15010025](https://doi.org/10.3390/cryst15010025)) | Sc on hand; **Zr** | yes |
| B30 | dosing check | 30 % 4047 in 6063 cups, Si ≈ 3.9 | Does measured Si follow the charge? | on hand | yes |
| B15 | dosing check, changed | Al + the Mn (or Zr) the S picks use, at a known level | Check that the element the agent picks depend on dissolves. Elemental Si only dissolved 29–44 % in 2–3.5 min at 738 °C ([#111](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/111)) | Mn on hand | yes |
| S1 | agent | **Al–4Mn–0.5Ti–0.5Zr** (Mair-type) | Sc-free. Mn supersaturation plus L1₂ Al₃(Ti,Zr) nucleants. Reported YS 284, UTS 320 MPa, 16.9 % elongation as-built, crack-free with no preheat at 380 W and 1900 mm/s ([10.1016/j.jallcom.2021.163156](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jallcom.2021.163156)). A different mechanism from D1 and D2 | Mn, Ti on hand; **Zr** | yes |
| S2 | agent | **an Fe-based eutectic**, e.g. Al–(3–5)Fe–1Mg–(0.5–0.7)Zr. If Fe stays capped at 0.5 wt%: **Al–10Ce** if Ce is ordered | Fe is cheap and not on the critical list. Reported YS 376, UTS 406 MPa, 11 % elongation after 400 °C/4 h ([10.1080/17452759.2025.2516663](https://doi.org/10.1080/17452759.2025.2516663)). Al–10Ce is printable and stable but weaker (YS ≈ 222 MPa, [10.1016/j.addma.2022.102959](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.addma.2022.102959)) | **Fe**, **Zr** (or **Ce**) | no (Fe or Ce cap) |
| S3, S4 | space-filling | from `seed_design.py --method imse` after the CALPHAD screen | Cover what D1, D2, S1 and S2 leave out. Today's picks from the on-hand elements are below | depends | yes |
| X1–X3 | flex | redo failed runs; otherwise early optimizer picks | — | — | — |

The rest of Edison's shortlist ([q2 table](edison/q2-seed-alloys-and-data/artifact-00.md)), in case
the feedstock or the freeze rules out S1 or S2:

- **Al–4Mn–1.3Mg–0.3Zr:** 99.6 % dense and crack-free. Hardness study only, no tensile data.
- **Al–Fe–Cr quasicrystal alloy:** YS 395 MPa as-built, but only 4 % elongation.
- **Addalloy-type Al–4.5Mg–1.5Zr:** YS ≈ 315 MPa. Over the Zr cap, and Mg evaporates.
- **Low-Sc Al–4.5Mg–0.3Sc–0.4Zr:** right on the #255 goal, but it sits next to D2. Leave the Sc
  axis to the optimizer: D2 and the Sc-free picks bracket it.
- **A20X-type Al–Cu–Ag–Mg–Ti–TiB₂:** needs Cu and Ag, and Ag isn't in the palette.

**With only the elements on hand** (Mn, Cr, Mg, Ti, Er, Zn, plus Si from 4047), the agent picks
fall back to Zr-free cousins such as Al–Mn–Cr or Al–Mn–Ti. They have weaker literature support,
because Zr is what suppresses cracking in most of these alloys. That is the case for getting Zr
in before Dec 7.

## Seeds for every node, not just compositions

BOFN keeps one GP per node, and each needs its own starting data. Edison found BOFN and pKGFN
papers that start from full-network evaluations (Astudillo and Frazier 2021; Buathong et al.
2023). Node-level initial designs in each node's own input space have also been published
(Kudva et al. 2026, MOBONS). The newer pKGFN formulation drops the rule that upstream nodes must
be evaluated first, which allows downstream data from other sources (Buathong and Frazier 2025)
([q1 §4](edison/q1-seeding-strategy/answer.md)). Most of that node-level data needs no atomizer
run.

| Node | Inputs → outputs | Seeds that cost no atomizer run | Seeds from atomizer runs | When |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CALPHAD descriptors | composition → liquidus, solidus, freezing range, Scheil cracking indices (Kou, CSC), phase fractions | A cheap, known function. Compute thousands of compositions with pycalphad now and Thermo-Calc once licensed ([#141](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/141)) | — | W1–W3 |
| Mineral burden | composition → weighted critical-mineral content | Analytic; freeze the weights first | — | G0 |
| Dosing and composition fidelity | charge recipe → measured composition (EDS, ICP-OES) | 6063 and 4047 as received | B30, B15, D1, D2, then every run | Dec 1–3 |
| Atomization | measured composition or its descriptors, superheat, amplitude → yield in cut, D10/D50/D90, sphericity, oxygen | Earlier runs (Oct 2, 6 and 8, and the 4047 runs in [#159](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/159)), tagged with their settings. Lang's relation as a prior mean for size, ± 20–30 % (q2) | A1–A5 (noise), then every run | from Nov 17 |
| Powder characterization (SEM/EDS) | powder → size and shape, satellites, homogeneity | Commercial AlSi10Mg 15–45 µm; the analysis pipeline from [#225](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/225) | Every run, at the Thursday session | weekly |
| Print parameters (tracks, cubes) | powder descriptors + power, speed, hatch, layer → melt-pool depth and width, mode, density, cracks | See the three sources below this table | In-house 6063 and D1 at P2; S-run tracks at P2 | P1 Dec 2–3, P2 Dec 16–17 |
| Hardness (the fast strength screen) | printed material, heat treatment → HV | P1 AlSi10Mg cubes, wrought 6063, published HV for the benchmarks | D1 and the S runs, from P2 and P3 | from Dec 11 |
| Tensile | printed material → yield strength, UTS, elongation | P1 AlSi10Mg bars. Literature values for the benchmarks and Sc-free alloys ([q2 table](edison/q2-seed-alloys-and-data/artifact-00.md)). Strengthening models ([q2](edison/q2-seed-alloys-and-data/artifact-02.md)), e.g. about 104 MPa from 3.7 wt% Mn kept in solid solution | Seeds from P3, then the finalists | Dec 14–16, Jan 19–22, Feb 9–12 |
| Corrosion | material → OCP, polarization | Wrought 6063 and printed AlSi10Mg, already in #256 | Finalists | when the electrodes arrive ([#221](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/221)) |

The print-parameter node has three sources that need no new alloy:

- **Literature.** The Barrionuevo LPBF density dataset in [`database-samples/`](../database-samples/)
  has 353 AlSi10Mg rows from 15 papers and 12 printers. 18 are on AconityLAB and 27 on a Concept
  Laser M2, the machine BYU has.
- **Models.** Eagar–Tsai and AM Module printability maps
  ([#262](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/262)).
- **P1.** Commercial AlSi10Mg single tracks in Sobol blocks, as in
  [#243](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/pull/243), plus cubes.

Two consequences:

- **The print-parameter node doesn't need new alloys to get started.** The atomizer runs only have
  to teach it how a new composition shifts the window. One build plate holds many parameter sets,
  so space-fill the print parameters on the plate, within the window the models predict.
- **Space-filling belongs in each node's own input space** (Edison q1, P6). A downstream GP sees
  CALPHAD descriptors and powder properties, not raw wt%. Once the CALPHAD screen exists, pick
  the space-filling seeds in descriptor space:
  `seed_design.py --candidates screen.csv --features ...`.

## Space-filling around the points we already have

[`seed_design.py`](seed_design.py) adds space-filling points around everything in
[`seeds.csv`](seeds.csv): 6063, D1, D2, B30 and B15. Add the agent picks there.

**The space.** It is the box a GP with `Normalize` sees: each element's wt% divided by its upper
bound. On top of that, each element one alloy has and the other doesn't adds 0.5 to the distance,
so different element sets count as further apart. Edison flagged plain Euclidean distance for
sparse compositions (q1, P5).

**The candidates:**

- The bounds are the finalized ones on [PR #72](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/pull/72):
  Al ≥ 85 wt%, a cap per element, a 0.10 wt% floor for any element that is switched on, and its
  joint caps except Mg + Si.
- Each candidate has one to three additions, drawn from the elements on hand
  ([#146](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/146)): Mn, Cr, Mg, Ti, Er
  and Zn, plus Si through 4047.
- Each has at least 3 wt% of additions in all. 6063 has about 1, D2 about 6 and AlSi10Mg about 10.

**The four methods:**

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `sobol` | First feasible points of a scrambled Sobol sequence, sampled face by face on the sparse simplex. Ignores the existing points |
| `sobol-exclusion` | Walks the same sequence and skips points within a radius of an existing or picked point (the heuristic in #275) |
| `maximin` | Greedy maximin (Kennard–Stone augmentation, Edison's recommendation): each pick is the candidate farthest from everything so far |
| `imse` | Greedy integrated-variance reduction: each pick most lowers the average variance of a GP over the whole feasible pool. Before any outcome is measured, that variance depends only on where the points are and on an assumed length scale (0.5) |

Three new points, averaged over 10 scrambles ([`results/space_filling_compare.csv`](results/space_filling_compare.csv)):

| Method | Nearest existing point ↑ | Nearest pair of new points ↑ | Fill distance ↓ | Mean distance to nearest point ↓ | Mean GP variance ↓ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| (existing points only) | | | 1.93 | 1.20 | 0.966 |
| `sobol` | 1.14 | 1.21 | 1.81 | 1.03 | 0.928 |
| `sobol-exclusion` | 1.14 | 1.21 | 1.81 | 1.03 | 0.928 |
| `maximin` | 1.78 | 2.10 | 1.72 | 1.11 | 0.955 |
| `imse` | 0.91 | 1.15 | 1.76 | **0.96** | **0.895** |

The picks for seed 0 ([`results/`](results/)):

| Method | SF1 (wt%) | SF2 (wt%) | SF3 (wt%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sobol`, `sobol-exclusion` | Al–2.72Cr–0.31Ti | Al–0.86Mn–2.12Cr–0.30Er | Al–4.57Mg–0.47Ti |
| `maximin` | Al–3.00Cr–0.50Er–7.45Zn | Al–4.44Mn–0.50Ti–7.06Zn | Al–4.86Mg–0.48Ti–0.45Er |
| `imse` | Al–3.22Mn–1.45Cr | Al–7.63Si–0.28Er | Al–3.41Si–4.91Zn |

What this shows:

- **Three points don't fill a 7-D space, whichever method picks them.** The best method lowers the
  mean GP variance from 0.97 to 0.90. The worst-covered composition stays almost as far from any
  experiment as before. In a reduced space, the same three runs cover much more: CALPHAD
  descriptors, or one or two sub-system families.
- **Maximin sends every point to a corner.** Al–3Cr–0.5Er–7.5Zn and Al–4.4Mn–0.5Ti–7.1Zn sit on
  several caps at once. They are the hardest of these alloys to melt, dose and print. They also
  cover the space worse on average than plain Sobol does. Maximin designs are known to hug the
  boundary. Edison recommended maximin; this is where I disagree with it.
- **Exclusion rarely bites with this few existing points.** With five points in 7-D, the first
  Sobol points are already well away from all of them, so `sobol` and `sobol-exclusion` pick the
  same alloys. Exclusion starts to matter once the existing set is large: literature points, or a
  dense CALPHAD screen.
- **`imse` covers best on average, and its picks are moderate alloys.** Al–3.2Mn–1.5Cr is a Zr-free
  cousin of the Al–Mn–Cr–Zr focus system. Use `imse`, but check its picks against the CALPHAD
  liquidus and cracking screen before dosing. Edison's objection to IMSE is that it needs a fitted
  GP. In fact it needs only kernel hyperparameters, but the length scale is a real choice. Rerun
  it with `--ell` set from the GP fitted to the A, B and D data once those exist.

## How many seeds: a toy check

[`budget_split_sim.py`](budget_split_sim.py) is a flat-GP toy, not a model of the campaign:

- **The space.** A 6-D unit box, where the response depends mostly on 3 hidden dimensions.
- **The response.** A "known family" bump of height 0.7, where the baselines sit (good, not
  best). A better bump of height 1.0 somewhere else, and a decoy.
- **The seeds.** The agent picks are drawn around the better bump ("agent right") or around the
  known family ("agent wrong"). One free weak point stands in for 6063.
- **The optimizer.** The remaining runs go to batches of 3, picked by qLogEI.
- **The runs.** 30 problem instances per scenario. Every split sees the same instances, so the
  differences are paired.

| Split (baselines + agent + space-filling) | Seeds | Best of 25, agent right | Best of 25, agent wrong | Paired difference vs 3 + 3 + 3, both scenarios | P(beat best baseline by 0.05) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 + 3 + 3 (proposed) | 9 | 0.935 | 0.822 | — | 0.55 |
| 2 + 2 + 2 | 6 | 0.960 | 0.864 | +0.034 ± 0.014 | 0.72 |
| **2 + 3 + 1** | 6 | 0.962 | 0.880 | **+0.043 ± 0.014** | **0.75** |
| 2 + 4 + 0 | 6 | **0.970** | 0.856 | +0.035 ± 0.017 | 0.70 |
| 2 + 0 + 4 | 6 | 0.869 | **0.892** | +0.003 ± 0.028 | 0.60 |
| 2 + 0 + 1 | 3 | 0.860 | 0.854 | −0.021 ± 0.020 | 0.57 |
| 3 + 3 + 6 | 12 | 0.952 | 0.845 | +0.020 ± 0.014 | 0.65 |
| 25 Sobol, no optimizer | 25 | 0.767 | 0.767 | −0.111 ± 0.030 | 0.43 |

The global maximum is about 1.0. ± is one standard error. Full results are in
[`results/budget_split/`](results/budget_split/).

What it says, within its assumptions:

- **About six seeds beat nine or twelve.** Three seeds (2 + 0 + 1) did a little worse than six,
  and spending all 25 runs on Sobol did worst.
- **Agent picks are worth a lot when they know something** (+0.10 when they're right) **and cost
  little when they don't.** They hurt mainly when they crowd the known family. 3 + 3 + 3 spends
  six of nine seeds there in the "wrong" case: three baselines and three agent picks.
- **2 + 3 + 1 was the most robust split.** It came near the top in both scenarios. 2 + 4 + 0 bets
  on the agent being right, and 2 + 0 + 4 bets on it being wrong.

What the toy leaves out, and why the real answer may need more seeds:

- In the toy the optimizer sees its result at once. In the campaign, strength comes back about
  four to six weeks after a run.
- Failed runs ([#274](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/274)).
- The function-network structure.
- A 15-element space.

So treat it as evidence on the direction, not on the exact number. It can be rerun on the 5-node
synthetic network in [#265](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/265)
once that exists.

## Literature and "fantasy" data

#275's "fantasy modelling" is synthetic or literature data that stands in until real data
exist. BoTorch's `fantasize` is something else: it conditions a model on sampled outcomes at
pending points, so that a batch doesn't pick the same point twice. The second meaning is what
[#104](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/104) is about, and what
pKGFN needs. To keep them apart, this folder calls the first kind **pseudo-data**. Edison calls
running the whole loop on it a "synthetic digital-twin dry run" (q1, P7).

How to use pseudo-data without fooling the model (Edison q1 §5, P8):

- **Give every row a `source`** (in-house, literature, database, model) and keep a separate noise
  level per source. Assuming one noise level for every source degrades multi-fidelity BO
  (Foumani et al. 2023).
- **Put it in through the model, not as if it were our own data.** Options:
  - a multi-task or multi-fidelity GP with the source as the task;
  - a prior mean from a physics model, with the GP learning the residual;
  - an RGPE-style ensemble, whose weight on the literature falls as our own data arrive.
- **Never overwrite a pseudo-data row with a real value.** Add the real row and let the source
  term take care of the rest. That keeps the replay honest, and it shows how far the priors were
  off.
- **Use it first for the dry run.** Run the whole loop on pseudo-data before Dec 18, so R1 isn't
  the first time the code sees a full network.

What each node can start from:

| Node | Pseudo-data source |
|---|---|
| Print parameters | Barrionuevo AlSi10Mg rows (local); NIST AM-Bench 2022 Al single tracks ([MDS2-2525](https://data.nist.gov/od/id/mds2-2525)); Eagar–Tsai with an absorptivity fitted to P1 tracks, accurate to about ± 20–30 % in conduction mode |
| Cracking | Scheil Kou index and CSC from CALPHAD, used as features or soft constraints |
| Strength | Literature tensile values (q2 table); solid-solution, Orowan and Hall–Petch terms, each about ± 15–25 % when retained solute and particle sizes are known |
| Atomization | Lang's relation, ± 20–30 % |

Taheri-Mousavi et al. (2024, [10.48550/arXiv.2406.17457](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2406.17457))
is the closest precedent. They used CALPHAD-derived descriptors and about 40 training
compositions with expected improvement to design an LPBF Al–Er–Zr–Ni alloy.

**Databases from #7 and #8**, sorted by node:

- **Print parameters:**
  - the Barrionuevo dataset (local, 1,579 rows, six alloys);
  - NIST AM-Bench 2022 (Al single tracks).
- **Strength:**
  - review tables: Aversa et al. 2019, [10.3390/ma12071007](https://doi.org/10.3390/ma12071007),
    and Liu et al. 2024, [10.1088/2631-7990/ad1657](https://doi.org/10.1088/2631-7990/ad1657);
  - the Luo 2024 AlSi10Mg process-structure-property set on Zenodo, listed in
    [`alloy-databases.md`](../alloy-databases.md);
  - an AlSi10Mg tensile set (Jatti et al., PLOS ONE, [10.1371/journal.pone.0324049](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0324049)).
- **Wrought and cast handbook data only:**
  - Knovel, Total Materia and MatWeb. These give the wrought 6063 baseline, not LPBF behaviour.
- **No use at these nodes:**
  - the DFT repositories (AFLOW, OQMD, JARVIS, NOMAD).

Edison couldn't verify the DOI it gave for a separate Barrionuevo AlSi10Mg data descriptor, so
check that DOI before using it.

## Making the seeds count for the paper

The schedule pre-registers an AI benchmark at G1 (Dec 4). Edison q1 (§6, P9) makes three points
about it:

- **Use one common seed set for every policy:** random, expert design of experiments, standard
  BO and BOFN. That set is the baselines and the space-filling seeds.
- **Count the agent picks on purpose.** Either put them in the common set, or charge them to the
  AI policy's budget. Report the warm-start effect and the optimizer's effect separately.
- **Replay only on points that were actually measured.** Anything else needs a clearly labelled,
  cross-validated simulator, and causal acceleration claims should be avoided.

With about 20 compositions, the acceleration factor will rest on that simulator. Space-filling
seeds make the simulator less wrong away from the optimizer's path. That is one more reason to
keep one or two of them.

## Pitfalls

From Edison q1's table ([artifact-01](edison/q1-seeding-strategy/artifact-01.md)) and this work:

| Pitfall | Do instead |
|---|---|
| Nine seeds leave only 12 optimizer runs | About 6–7 seeds |
| A 10d rule would need 140–150 runs in 15-D | Shrink the space before atomizing: at most 3–4 additions, CALPHAD descriptors as GP inputs, sparse kernels |
| Agent picks cluster around Al–Si–Mg and Al–Mg–Sc–Zr | Two picks, with different mechanisms and element sets, chosen away from D1 and D2 |
| Sobol in the full 15-element simplex is almost never feasible | Sample face by face on the sparse simplex (as `seed_design.py` does) |
| Maximin picks extreme corners | `imse`, or maximin only after the CALPHAD screen trims the pool |
| Euclidean distance ignores element identity | Add an element-set term (`--set-weight`) |
| Composition-only space-filling leaves the downstream nodes cold | Seed each node from its own cheap sources; space-fill in descriptor and print-parameter space |
| Pseudo-data pooled with real data biases the model | A source column, per-source noise, multi-task or multi-fidelity; never overwrite rows |
| Seeds differ between the compared policies | One common seed set; report warm-start and optimizer effects separately |
| The seeds need elements we don't have | Check Zr, Fe and Ce now; B15 checks the element the S picks depend on |
| Failed runs dropped from the data | Record failures as outcomes ([#274](https://github.com/vertical-cloud-lab/digital-alloy-lab/issues/274)) |

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Pick space-filling seed compositions around the points already chosen (#275).

#275 suggests taking Sobol points but throwing out the ones that land too close to existing
experiments. This script does that, plus two more model-based variants, in the space a GP
with a ``Normalize`` input transform over the design box would see (each element's wt%
divided by its upper bound), plus ``--set-weight`` (default 0.5) for every element that one
alloy has and the other doesn't, so different element sets count as further apart:

- ``sobol``: the first n feasible points of a scrambled Sobol sequence. Ignores the existing
  points; this is the plain baseline.
- ``sobol-exclusion``: walk the same Sobol sequence and skip any point closer than ``--radius``
  to an existing or already-picked point (the heuristic in #275).
- ``maximin``: greedy maximin augmentation over a large Sobol candidate pool. Each pick is the
  candidate farthest from its nearest existing or picked point.
- ``imse`` (default): greedy integrated-variance reduction. Each pick is the candidate that most
  lowers the average posterior variance of a GP (RBF kernel, fixed length scale) over the whole
  feasible pool, given the existing and picked points. Before any outcome is measured the GP
  variance depends only on where the points are, so this needs no data. Unlike maximin it
  doesn't push every pick into a corner of the box.

The design space follows the finalized element bounds on PR #72 (Edison task ``caec5419``):
Al balance at least 85 wt%, the recommended upper bound per element, a 0.10 wt% floor for any
element that is switched on, and the joint caps (Mn+Cr <= 7, Sc+Zr <= 1.5, Cu+Mg <= 5,
Cu+Li <= 4, Mg+Zn+Li <= 10 wt%). Mg+Si <= 6 is left out on purpose, because AlSi10Mg, the
benchmark, breaks it. Each candidate has at most ``--k-max`` additions (sparse sub-systems)
and at least ``--min-total`` wt% of additions in all (default 3; 6063 has about 1, the
Scalmalloy-type benchmark about 6, AlSi10Mg about 10).

Existing points come from ``seeds.csv`` (baselines, dosing checks, agent picks; use measured
compositions once there are any). The default element set is what is on hand or shipping per
#146 on 2026-11-13: Mn, Cr, Mg, Ti, Er and Zn from ESPI, plus Si through 4047 powder. Sn (cap
0.1 wt%) and Sc (the mineral the campaign is trying to avoid; D2 already covers it) are left
out. Add Zr with ``--elements ... Zr`` once it is on the shelf.

After the CALPHAD screen, pick in descriptor space instead of composition space, since that
is what the downstream nodes take as input:

    python bofn-seeding/seed_design.py --candidates screen.csv --features freezing_range csc

``screen.csv`` needs the feature columns, and an ``existing`` column set to 1 on the rows
that are already chosen (benchmarks, agent picks).

Usage:
    python bofn-seeding/seed_design.py                     # 3 picks, imse, default elements
    python bofn-seeding/seed_design.py --n 4 --method maximin
    python bofn-seeding/seed_design.py --compare           # every method, averaged over scrambles
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import csv
import itertools
import pathlib
import sys

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import qmc

HERE = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent

PALETTE = ["Mn", "Cr", "Zr", "Mg", "Si", "Cu", "Ti", "Fe", "Ni", "Ce", "Sc", "Li", "Er", "Zn", "Sn"]
# Recommended upper bounds in wt% (PR #72, "02_finalized_bounds_table.md").
UPPER_WT = {
    "Mn": 5.0, "Cr": 3.0, "Zr": 1.0, "Mg": 5.0, "Si": 12.0, "Cu": 4.0, "Ti": 0.5, "Fe": 0.5,
    "Ni": 0.5, "Ce": 6.0, "Sc": 0.8, "Li": 2.0, "Er": 0.5, "Zn": 8.0, "Sn": 0.1,
}
AL_MIN_WT = 85.0
FLOOR_WT = 0.10
JOINT_CAPS = [
    (("Mn", "Cr"), 7.0),
    (("Sc", "Zr"), 1.5),
    (("Cu", "Mg"), 5.0),
    (("Cu", "Li"), 4.0),
    (("Mg", "Zn", "Li"), 10.0),
]
ATOMIC_WEIGHT = {
    "Al": 26.982, "Mn": 54.938, "Cr": 51.996, "Zr": 91.224, "Mg": 24.305, "Si": 28.085,
    "Cu": 63.546, "Ti": 47.867, "Fe": 55.845, "Ni": 58.693, "Ce": 140.116, "Sc": 44.956,
    "Li": 6.94, "Er": 167.259, "Zn": 65.38, "Sn": 118.71,
}
DEFAULT_ELEMENTS = ["Mn", "Cr", "Mg", "Si", "Er", "Ti", "Zn"]
UB = np.array([UPPER_WT[e] for e in PALETTE])
IDX = {e: i for i, e in enumerate(PALETTE)}
METHODS = ["sobol", "sobol-exclusion", "maximin", "imse"]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- design space
def feasible(W: np.ndarray, min_total: float = 0.0, tol: float = 1e-9) -> np.ndarray:
    """Rows of W (wt% of each palette element) that satisfy the bounds and joint caps."""
    ok = (W <= UB + tol).all(axis=1) & (W >= -tol).all(axis=1)
    ok &= W.sum(axis=1) <= 100.0 - AL_MIN_WT + tol
    ok &= W.sum(axis=1) >= min_total - tol
    ok &= ((W == 0) | (W >= FLOOR_WT - tol)).all(axis=1)
    for elements, cap in JOINT_CAPS:
        ok &= W[:, [IDX[e] for e in elements]].sum(axis=1) <= cap + tol
    return ok


def candidate_pool(elements, k_min, k_max, per_subsystem, seed, min_total=0.0):
    """Feasible sparse compositions, interleaved across sub-systems in Sobol order.

    Every sub-system (k additions out of ``elements``) gets its own scrambled Sobol sequence
    over [floor, upper bound]^k. Round-robin over the sub-systems turns them into one
    sequence, so "the first n Sobol points" is well defined for the sobol methods.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    subsystems = [c for k in range(k_min, k_max + 1) for c in itertools.combinations(elements, k)]
    rng.shuffle(subsystems)
    m = int(np.ceil(np.log2(per_subsystem)))
    streams = []
    for sub in subsystems:
        u = qmc.Sobol(d=len(sub), scramble=True, seed=rng).random_base2(m)
        lo = np.full(len(sub), FLOOR_WT)
        hi = np.array([UPPER_WT[e] for e in sub])
        W = np.zeros((len(u), len(PALETTE)))
        W[:, [IDX[e] for e in sub]] = lo + u * (hi - lo)
        streams.append(W[feasible(W, min_total)])
    rows, labels = [], []
    for i in range(max(len(s) for s in streams)):
        for sub, s in zip(subsystems, streams):
            if i < len(s):
                rows.append(s[i])
                labels.append("Al-" + "-".join(sub))
    return np.array(rows), labels


def read_existing(path):
    with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))
    W = np.array([[float(r.get(e) or 0) for e in PALETTE] for r in rows])
    return W, rows


def features(W, set_weight):
    """Normalized wt% plus set_weight x (element switched on): a mixed distance.

    Squared distance = range-scaled Euclidean + set_weight^2 x (number of elements in one alloy
    but not the other), so alloys with different element sets count as further apart (#275,
    Edison q1, pitfall P5).
    """
    return np.hstack([W / UB, set_weight * (W > 0)])


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- selection
def _sqdist(A, B):
    return np.maximum((A * A).sum(1)[:, None] + (B * B).sum(1)[None, :] - 2 * A @ B.T, 0.0)


def _rbf(A, B, ell):
    return np.exp(-0.5 * _sqdist(A, B) / ell**2)


def select_sobol(Xc, Xe, n, **_):
    return list(range(min(n, len(Xc))))


def select_exclusion(Xc, Xe, n, radius, **_):
    picked = []
    design = Xe.copy()
    for i, x in enumerate(Xc):
        if len(design) == 0 or np.sqrt(_sqdist(x[None], design).min()) >= radius:
            picked.append(i)
            design = np.vstack([design, x])
            if len(picked) == n:
                break
    return picked


def select_maximin(Xc, Xe, n, **_):
    dmin = np.sqrt(_sqdist(Xc, Xe).min(1)) if len(Xe) else np.full(len(Xc), np.inf)
    picked = []
    for _ in range(n):
        i = int(np.argmax(dmin))
        picked.append(i)
        dmin = np.minimum(dmin, np.sqrt(_sqdist(Xc, Xc[i : i + 1])[:, 0]))
    return picked


def posterior_var(Xr, Xd, ell, jitter=1e-6):
    """Prior-unit GP posterior variance at Xr given noise-free points Xd (locations only)."""
    if len(Xd) == 0:
        return np.ones(len(Xr))
    L = np.linalg.cholesky(_rbf(Xd, Xd, ell) + jitter * np.eye(len(Xd)))
    V = np.linalg.solve(L, _rbf(Xd, Xr, ell))
    return np.clip(1.0 - (V * V).sum(0), 0.0, 1.0)


def select_imse(Xc, Xe, n, ell, n_ref=1500, seed=0, jitter=1e-6, **_):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    Xr = Xc[rng.choice(len(Xc), size=min(n_ref, len(Xc)), replace=False)]
    picked = []
    for _ in range(n):
        Xd = np.vstack([Xe] + [Xc[picked]]) if (len(Xe) or picked) else np.zeros((0, Xc.shape[1]))
        Krc = _rbf(Xr, Xc, ell)
        if len(Xd):
            L = np.linalg.cholesky(_rbf(Xd, Xd, ell) + jitter * np.eye(len(Xd)))
            A = np.linalg.solve(L, _rbf(Xd, Xc, ell))  # (d, M)
            B = np.linalg.solve(L, _rbf(Xd, Xr, ell))  # (d, R)
            cov = Krc - B.T @ A
            var_c = np.clip(1.0 - (A * A).sum(0), 1e-12, None)
        else:
            cov, var_c = Krc, np.ones(len(Xc))
        gain = (cov * cov).mean(0) / var_c
        gain[picked] = -np.inf
        picked.append(int(np.argmax(gain)))
    return picked


SELECT = {"sobol": select_sobol, "sobol-exclusion": select_exclusion, "maximin": select_maximin, "imse": select_imse}


def coverage(Xe, Xn, Xr, ell):
    """How well existing + new points cover a reference pool of feasible points."""
    D = np.vstack([Xe, Xn])
    near = np.sqrt(_sqdist(Xr, D).min(1))
    gap_existing = np.sqrt(_sqdist(Xn, Xe).min()) if len(Xe) else np.nan
    gap_new = np.sqrt(_sqdist(Xn, Xn)[np.triu_indices(len(Xn), 1)].min()) if len(Xn) > 1 else np.nan
    return {
        "nearest_to_existing": gap_existing,
        "nearest_new_pair": gap_new,
        "fill_distance": near.max(),
        "mean_nearest": near.mean(),
        "mean_post_var": posterior_var(Xr, D, ell).mean(),
    }


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- output
def at_percent(w):
    mol = {e: w[IDX[e]] / ATOMIC_WEIGHT[e] for e in PALETTE if w[IDX[e]] > 0}
    mol["Al"] = (100.0 - w.sum()) / ATOMIC_WEIGHT["Al"]
    tot = sum(mol.values())
    return {e: 100.0 * v / tot for e, v in mol.items()}


def label(w):
    parts = [f"{w[IDX[e]]:.2f}{e}" for e in PALETTE if w[IDX[e]] > 0]
    return "Al-" + "-".join(parts) if parts else "Al"


def run_composition(args):
    We, rows = read_existing(args.existing)
    Wc, subs = candidate_pool(args.elements, args.k_min, args.k_max, args.per_subsystem, args.seed, args.min_total)
    Xc, Xe = features(Wc, args.set_weight), features(We, args.set_weight)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(args.seed + 1)
    Wr, _ = candidate_pool(args.elements, args.k_min, args.k_max, 256, args.seed + 1000, args.min_total)
    Xr = features(Wr, args.set_weight)
    Xr = Xr[rng.choice(len(Xr), size=min(3000, len(Xr)), replace=False)]
    print(f"design space: Al + {args.k_min}-{args.k_max} of {', '.join(args.elements)}, "
          f"total additions {args.min_total:g}-{100 - AL_MIN_WT:g} wt%; "
          f"{len(Xc)} feasible candidates; {len(Xe)} existing points from {args.existing.name}")

    if args.compare:
        compare(Xc, Xe, Xr, args)
        return
    picked = SELECT[args.method](Xc, Xe, args.n, radius=args.radius, ell=args.ell, seed=args.seed)
    Wn = Wc[picked]
    assert feasible(Wn, args.min_total).all()
    cov = coverage(Xe, Xc[picked], Xr, args.ell)
    out = []
    for j, i in enumerate(picked):
        d = np.sqrt(_sqdist(Xc[i : i + 1], Xe)[0]) if len(Xe) else np.array([np.nan])
        k = int(np.argmin(d))
        atp = at_percent(Wc[i])
        out.append({
            "code": f"SF{j + 1}", "strategy": "space-filling", "method": args.method,
            "subsystem": subs[i], "wt_pct": label(Wc[i]),
            "at_pct": "Al-" + "-".join(f"{atp[e]:.2f}{e}" for e in PALETTE if e in atp),
            "nearest_existing": rows[k]["code"] if len(Xe) else "", "distance": round(float(d[k]), 3),
            **{e: round(float(Wc[i, IDX[e]]), 3) for e in PALETTE},
        })
    print(f"\n{args.method}: {args.n} picks (distance: wt% scaled by each upper bound, plus {args.set_weight:g} per element in one alloy but not the other)")
    for r in out:
        print(f"  {r['code']}: {r['wt_pct']:<36} wt%   nearest existing {r['nearest_existing']} at {r['distance']}")
    print("  coverage: " + ", ".join(f"{k} {v:.3f}" for k, v in cov.items()))
    if args.out:
        args.out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        with open(args.out, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=list(out[0]))
            w.writeheader()
            w.writerows(out)
        print(f"wrote {args.out}")


def compare(Xc, Xe, Xr, args):
    """Average coverage of every method over several scrambles of the Sobol pool."""
    results = {m: [] for m in METHODS}
    for s in range(args.repeats):
        Wc, _ = candidate_pool(args.elements, args.k_min, args.k_max, args.per_subsystem, args.seed + 17 * s, args.min_total)
        Xc_s = features(Wc, args.set_weight)
        for m in METHODS:
            picked = SELECT[m](Xc_s, Xe, args.n, radius=args.radius, ell=args.ell, seed=s)
            results[m].append(coverage(Xe, Xc_s[picked], Xr, args.ell))
    keys = list(results[METHODS[0]][0])
    print(f"\n{args.n} new points, mean over {args.repeats} scrambles (higher is better for the first two, lower for the rest)")
    print(f"{'method':<16}" + "".join(f"{k:>21}" for k in keys))
    for m in METHODS:
        print(f"{m:<16}" + "".join(f"{np.nanmean([r[k] for r in results[m]]):>21.3f}" for k in keys))
    base = posterior_var(Xr, Xe, args.ell).mean()
    print(f"{'(existing only)':<16}" + f"{'':>21}{'':>21}"
          f"{np.sqrt(_sqdist(Xr, Xe).min(1)).max():>21.3f}{np.sqrt(_sqdist(Xr, Xe).min(1)).mean():>21.3f}{base:>21.3f}")
    if args.out:
        args.out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        with open(args.out, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            w = csv.writer(f)
            w.writerow(["method", *keys])
            for m in METHODS:
                w.writerow([m, *(round(float(np.nanmean([r[k] for r in results[m]])), 4) for k in keys)])
        print(f"wrote {args.out}")


def run_features(args):
    with open(args.candidates, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))
    F = np.array([[float(r[c]) for c in args.features] for r in rows])
    lo, hi = F.min(0), F.max(0)
    X = (F - lo) / np.where(hi > lo, hi - lo, 1.0)
    is_existing = np.array([str(r.get("existing", "0")).strip() in {"1", "true", "True", "yes"} for r in rows])
    Xe, Xc = X[is_existing], X[~is_existing]
    cand_rows = [r for r, e in zip(rows, is_existing) if not e]
    picked = SELECT[args.method](Xc, Xe, args.n, radius=args.radius, ell=args.ell, seed=args.seed)
    print(f"{len(Xc)} candidates, {len(Xe)} existing; {args.method} in ({', '.join(args.features)}) space:")
    for i in picked:
        d = np.sqrt(_sqdist(Xc[i : i + 1], Xe).min()) if len(Xe) else float("nan")
        print(f"  {cand_rows[i].get('code', i)}: " + ", ".join(f"{c}={cand_rows[i][c]}" for c in args.features)
              + f"  (nearest existing {d:.3f})")
    if args.out:
        args.out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        with open(args.out, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=list(cand_rows[0]))
            w.writeheader()
            w.writerows(cand_rows[i] for i in picked)
        print(f"wrote {args.out}")


def main(argv=None):
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    p.add_argument("--n", type=int, default=3, help="how many space-filling points to add")
    p.add_argument("--method", choices=METHODS, default="imse")
    p.add_argument("--elements", nargs="+", default=DEFAULT_ELEMENTS, choices=PALETTE)
    p.add_argument("--k-min", type=int, default=1, help="fewest additions per alloy")
    p.add_argument("--k-max", type=int, default=3, help="most additions per alloy")
    p.add_argument("--min-total", type=float, default=3.0,
                   help="least total wt%% of additions; keeps picks out of the dilute corner near 6063 "
                        "(about 1 wt%%), which can't be strong. 0 turns it off")
    p.add_argument("--per-subsystem", type=int, default=256, help="Sobol points per sub-system (rounded up to 2^m)")
    p.add_argument("--existing", type=pathlib.Path, default=HERE / "seeds.csv")
    p.add_argument("--radius", type=float, default=0.5, help="exclusion radius for sobol-exclusion (normalized units)")
    p.add_argument("--ell", type=float, default=0.5, help="RBF length scale for imse and the coverage metric (normalized units)")
    p.add_argument("--set-weight", type=float, default=0.5,
                   help="weight on element-set differences in the distance (0 = plain range-scaled Euclidean)")
    p.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=0)
    p.add_argument("--compare", action="store_true", help="compare all methods instead of picking")
    p.add_argument("--repeats", type=int, default=10, help="scrambles to average over with --compare")
    p.add_argument("--candidates", type=pathlib.Path, help="CSV of screened candidates (descriptor-space mode)")
    p.add_argument("--features", nargs="+", help="feature columns of --candidates to space-fill in")
    p.add_argument("--out", type=pathlib.Path, help="write the picks (or the comparison) to this CSV")
    args = p.parse_args(argv)
    if args.candidates:
        if not args.features:
            sys.exit("--candidates needs --features")
        run_features(args)
    else:
        run_composition(args)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
